Speech enhancement is typically approached by recovering lost audio information from time-frequency patterns in a mask-based method.

Deep learning models have generally focused on extracting features from contiguous time-domain segments for the recovery process.

In this research, we approach speech enhancement from a unique perspective by treating time-frequency patterns as signal dependencies.

We propose a novel model called DPCRN, which leverages two convolutional neural network structures to extract features from time-frequency patterns.

Unlike conventional methods that process data in a linear manner, our model utilizes a non-linear attention mechanism to re-rank importance across frequency and time dimensions.

By guiding subsequent feature extraction through dynamic attention maps, we achieve a more efficient focus on the most relevant patterns.

We further enhance performance by incorporating an adaptive gate that automatically adjusts the influence of historical spectral estimates on current predictions.

This gate allows the model to retain useful information from previous time frames while filtering out inconsistent patterns.

Our model was evaluated on two public datasets and demonstrated state-of-the-art results at high noise levels in full-duplex wireless scenarios.

Additionally, DPCRN exhibited superior generalization capabilities, exhibiting up to a 6.54 dB improvement in SNRIS for unseen high noise levels.

Detailed comparisons of the turn-around radii and mass profiles of 13 cluster-void pairs provide a significant constraint on modified gravity theories, specifically for $f(R)$ gravity. By combining this information with the dark energy equation of state, we can minimize the models' parameters. Our analysis shows that the current data are consistent with $\Lambda$CDM at a 1-sigma level, while modified gravity models are only 2-sigma away, making them a viable alternative to the standard model. Furthermore, the turn-around radii statistics and descriptions have no significant differences compared to $\Lambda$CDM, at a 2-sigma level, thus breaking the degeneracy between dark sector parameters. To further reduce degeneracy within modified gravity models, we propose using the matter power spectrum as an additional probe.

We investigated the limitations of using the classic analogy between fluid dynamics and heat flow in the study of convection. Although this concept has value in providing a simplified view, we believe it has hindered researchers from exploring more accurate models. To address this issue, we developed a new, mathematically rigorous model consisting of two coupled components that describe the interaction between convective turbulence and coherent structures. Surprisingly, this model successfully predicts key characteristics of convection, including a specific scaling of heat flux that traditional theories could not, without making exceptional assumptions. Notably, this unusual scaling emerges naturally when the energy dissipated by the coherent structures become dominant. Furthermore, this distinct regime arises through gradual and predictable means.

We've configured a one-dimensional system where a moving particle enters a cavity and interacts with an atom inside, which is also connected to a second atom a distance $a$ away. By analyzing how both the motion of the particle and the interaction affect the system, we discovered that even if the cavity becomes entangled with an atom, there's no need for the atoms themselves to be correlated in order to create entanglement among them as the system evolves. In fact, the more interconnected the cavity and the incoming atom are, the more rapidly this atomic entanglement can be generated, giving us a straightforward method to generate highly interconnected states, including states where three or more atoms are deeply entangled, by simply letting the system run for a set amount of time. Furthermore, if the cavity has significant losses, we found that this could actually impede the generation of this multi-particle entanglement, which presents an obstacle to using this method in real-world applications. In addition, we examined how introducing more particles into the cavity influences the system, and we observed that increasing this number can both accelerate and decelerate the generation of this multi-particle entanglement, which suggests that there's an ideal number of particles that could be most effective at achieving this.

This paper provides an overview of the advancements made to the silicon pixel detector of the CMS detector since 2016, when only the forward sections had been upgraded with novel silicon pixel detectors (NOPix1), while the primary sampling and forward sections (PIXE) utilized the older NPCI1 technology. Following 2016, substantial upgrades were undertaken to upgrade the remaining sections of the detector, significantly boosting its performance for the remaining years of the Phase-II upgrade plan, notably by upgrading about 8000 silicon pixel and nitrogen cathode trace tubes. Following 2016, substantial upgrades were undertaken to the silicon pixel detector following 2016, when only the first few sections were upgraded with a compact silicon pixel detector following 2016, while the rest used the older nitrogen-cooled trace tubes. Following 2016, substantial upgrades were undertaken to the front-end electronics (digi-tubes) following 2016, while the rest used the older nitrogen-cooled trace tubes. We will discuss how the new design of the detector and upgrades followed 2016, while the rest used the older nitrogen-cooled trace tubes, will significantly improve the performance of the detector and upgrades followed 2016, while the rest used the older nitrogen-cooled trace tubes, and lessons learned from the following 2016, while the rest used the older nitrogen-cooled trace tubes.

Using the AdS/CMT correspondence, we construct a (1,1/2)-form vector for pure glue using the field strength, which allows us to calculate a glueball spectrum. Our method yields masses that are in good agreement with existing pure glue results, assuming a linear relation between the form vector components and an appropriate choice of the mass dimension parameter. This suggests that the proposed form may capture key features of QCD that are not fully described within the perturbative regime.

Social media platforms offer a range of tools to gather essential information, 
including sentiment analysis, which is crucial for understanding public opinion. 
This research evaluates the effectiveness of using pre-trained BERT transformers 
and custom-designed LSTM networks in analyzing the sentiment of tweets. We compare 
multiple LSTM configurations, focusing on different attention mechanisms and techniques 
to handle sequence data. Our experiments, conducted on two distinct datasets, 
demonstrate that integrating CBLM attention with bag-of-words representation yields 
an impressive 94.64% accuracy. This approach outperforms other methods, 
achieved through a systematic exploration of attention mechanisms and 
sequence-handling techniques within LSTM networks.

Using dynamical variables, we re-examine the AdS/CMT correspondence to explore
the link between quark-gluon plasma and black holes in AdS space within a modified
theory of gravity. We determine the impact of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on
the shadow radius, thermal profile, and charge of black holes in four-dimensional
anti-de Sitter space. Our analysis shows that as the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter increases,
both the shadow radius and temperature of black holes decrease, whereas the charge of black holes increases.
Furthermore, our findings suggest that the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter can explain the observed
properties of the quark-gluon plasma, specifically its shadow radius and temperature.

Quantum state characterization through optical tomography is explored using Heisenberg image analysis, which allows for a comprehensive understanding of a state's nature. By leveraging the connectivity between optical tomography and photometric measurements, we can incorporate simple, intuitive tools to study the nonclassical properties of quantum states. This approach enables the representation of a state's coherence, entanglement, and particle-like properties in the same framework as its Wigner function, thus facilitating a unified analysis. The methodology is demonstrated through the examination of both single-qubit states and the Mollow triplet within the context of an atom interacting with the electromagnetic field. The resulting descriptions are derived from direct measurements, rather than theoretical calculations, and the resulting analysis reveals that entanglement fluctuations and nonclassical state dynamics can be understood in a unified framework. Finally, the connection between our approach and quantum erasure is established through the use of photometric data, thus providing a basis for analyzing quantum state reconstruction and the emergence of interference patterns in both the momentum position space and the intensity distribution.

The success of using large language models in dialogue tasks largely depends on the guidelines provided, particularly the specification of their function or role in the conversation. To measure the impact of these guidelines on general dialogue applications, we trained five commercial dialogue models with varying levels of instruction clarity in a range of general dialogue scenarios. Our study showed that the performance of these models was significantly influenced by the clarity of their stated role, particularly in scenarios where their function was ambiguous or overly specific. Our experiment results underscore the critical role of clear instruction provision when employing large language models in most dialogue applications.

Implementing precise disease detection and forecasting tools can improve farm productivity and profitability by reducing unnecessary pesticide use, lowering production costs, and increasing yields. However, creating effective models requires access to historical data from various sources, including yield data, profit records, and disease pressure measurements. This research highlights the challenges of gathering this data and explores potential solutions. We also outline critical considerations for applying data science and machine learning methods to agricultural problems, with a focus on the difficulty of obtaining comprehensive datasets and the importance of stakeholder engagement in the data collection process. Using commercial strawberry farming as an example, we discuss the challenges of gathering relevant data and the potential difficulties these challenges pose for developing effective predictive models. The difficulties faced in gathering comprehensive datasets and the problems these data acquisition challenges create for developing effective machine learning models in the context of commercial strawberry farming and disease management.

As 5G technology advances, high-resolution panoramic and 360-degree videos are becoming more feasible, but these videos consume significant bandwidth and require precise viewport prediction to optimize encoding. In this study, we investigate the use of video subtitles as a novel feature for enhancing the accuracy of viewport prediction. A new dataset, VueSub, has been created to experiment with this hypothesis. The results showed that incorporating subtitle information into machine learning models, particularly those using a deep learning approach, significantly improves the accuracy of viewport prediction when user interactions are limited.

We have developed a precise and computationally feasible procedure for creating projected operator product state (PEPO) representations that are suitable for simulating the thermal properties and time evolution of one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions in the periodic boundary condition. By employing a structured product of graph states and unitary gates, we are able to create PEPOs whose bond dimensions are not excessively large relative to the number of site numbers per loop, and which can also effectively approximate thermal states and time-evolved systems with high accuracy. Furthermore, our constructed PEPOs possess certain characteristics that enable them to be utilized as prepared states in projective measurements, thereby yielding equal results for both thermal expectation values and real-time dynamics. Notably, our numerical studies suggest that the bond dimensions of the PEPOs required to capture the characteristics of thermal states and time evolution may scale as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\beta/J})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\log t)$, respectively.

Using Taylor series expansions, we establish a decoupling inequality for canonical surfaces that exhibit a specific lower bound on curvature, following the methodology set by Demeter, Guth, and others; we then refine this inequality to apply to a broader class of surfaces through direct comparison, bypassing some distance estimates popularized by others.

This paper introduces a novel concept of anisotropic capacity corresponding to the classical electric capacity. Lebesgue's isodiametric inequality for ellipsoids and Falconer's bound for ball volumes are adapted to this new context. Additionally, specific questions from our previous preprint are addressed within the framework of anisotropy.

This paper outlines key background information related to glitches. Glitches are sudden spikes or dips in data that occur very rarely and are caused by transient disturbances in the system. These issues have impacted the ATLAS experiment's measurements of accelerations throughout the years, with some even influencing notable physics results like the discovery of new particles. We have gathered all known instances of glitches from 2011 to 2019 and provided a comprehensive table. Additionally, we have explained the mechanisms behind several of these glitches and discussed potential strategies for mitigation.

Many soft matter systems exhibit complex movements due to an interplay between self-propulsion and flexible structures. To better understand these active dimers, we propose a general framework that can accommodate various configurations of flexible components. Our analysis shows that even when the flexible parts are not identical, the movement can still be broken down into two distinct parts: forward motion and side-to-side motion. We use a microfluidic device composed of two rotating wheels to demonstrate this concept, resulting in a novel method of miniature actuation. This setup serves as an accessible tool for testing hydrodynamic theories and can be customized to study different dynamic scenarios.

This paper examines the k-strong shortest path union cover problem, where k non-overlapping subgraphs must be identified to cover all short paths between node pairs up to a given length l in a graph G. Various applications, including establishing resilient and redundant network connections, highlight the importance of this problem. Unfortunately, no precise solution method is known due to its computational difficulty. Our research offers two main contributions. Firstly, we confirm that the problem belongs to the complexity class KC. Secondly, for the case where l is small, two tailored heuristic methods are proposed to efficiently find a cover with fewer than k subgraphs. These heuristics combine elements of strong shortest path decomposition, minimum strong shortest path cover, and minimum strong shortest path tree cover. Three sets of experiments compare different parameters and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

Using the QCD sum rule method, we have directly calculated the second moment of the gluon distribution for the proton's spin polarization, utilizing the anomalous dimension of the corresponding twist-2 polarized gluon conjugate operator. To assess the approach's reliability, the typical QCD sum rule indicators - the operator product expansion convergence, the contour integration independence, and the duality variance - were evaluated, resulting in an estimated total uncertainty of ~50% for the distribution. This substantial ambiguity mostly originates from infrared renormalons and can be minimized by incorporating the theoretical uncertainty from renormalons into the estimate. By factoring in both the parametric and numerical uncertainties, we obtained a specific numerical range for the distribution at various scale points, specifically for Q^2 = 0.36, 1.0, and 2.25 GeV^2. Nevertheless, the large uncertainty renders a more precise assessment of the gluon contribution to the proton's spin essential, particularly when considering the significantly uncertain parameter F_g(μ^2) = (1/π)∫_0^(1-ε) dx x^2 Δg(x,μ^2).

We investigate the relationship between a tree's structure and the frog model's transient or recurrent behavior. Specifically, we focus on simple trees where we demonstrate that above certain degree thresholds, the model becomes transient or recurrent based on the values of $k$. Notably, for the binary tree, we identify precise ranges of $k$ below which the model remains transient for any initial condition and in which it is recurrent when the initial condition exceeds a certain value. Additionally, we find an infinite range of $k$ values where the model's behavior is transient when the initial condition is limited to certain values and recurrent when the initial condition surpasses a certain value. On the other hand, we also find an infinite range of $k$ values where the model's behavior is transient when the initial condition is limited to certain values and recurrent when the initial condition surpasses a certain value.

This study investigates a one-dimensional magnetophotonic crystal composed of dielectric layers with a surface covered in a metal film. We utilize a modification of Adams's matrix method to analyze the system's properties. By examining the surface of an L-shaped region and employing a uniqueness theorem, we achieve a non-singular impedance function. Furthermore, we investigate how a ray anomaly and surface plasmons on the metal film interact. We demonstrate that this interference results in distinct line shapes, including asymmetric types as well as shifted or eliminated anomalous lines. Additionally, we show that an external magnetic field can influence these line shapes, leading to their extinction or splitting into two lines with different frequencies.

We investigate Black-box knowledge distillation under attack conditions, or "decision-based" (DB3) scenarios, and discover that it offers a significant advantage over conventional knowledge distillation approaches. In other words, we can create a highly efficient classified image net (CIFAR-10) classifier in just a few query attempts to a designated black-box neural network and understand its decision-making process. In contrast, conventional knowledge distillation methods require many more samples. Interestingly, we can also successfully train a efficient classifier based on the attacked network's knowledge, which significantly outperforms the original black-box network. We demonstrate these findings by experimenting on real and artificially altered networks, with attacks simulating common ones such as decision-based adaptive training (DAT), network training attack (NTA), and clean network attack (CNA).

The Faraday Rotation Experiment at the DAΦNE factory has provided precise measurements of branching fractions and correlation matrices for the decay of $η_η_c$ into two photons. These studies have been conducted using two distinct methods: the direct method and the indirect method. Here, a third approach, termed the hybrid method, has been explored. By taking into account the experimental and model-based uncertainties more thoroughly, the hybrid method combines elements from both direct and indirect approaches. The new approach considers the full uncertainty structures available from data, while also incorporating prior knowledge of correlation matrices. As a result, more accurate estimates of uncertainty can be achieved, making the branching fractions and correlation matrix measurements more reliable.

Given a multiplicity-free module $M$ within a specific category $\mathcal{O}$ for the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, specific properties allow for the full reconstruction of its submodule lattice. This paper demonstrates that a multiplicity-free property is essential for such reconstruction and provides a detailed analysis of the factors composing $M$'s lattice. It achieves this by leveraging the $\mathbb{Z}$-graded structure of $M$ and applying a previously established $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-invariant map.

Given a graph $G$ and a collection of its vertices $S$, the Strong Geodetic
Recognition Problem involves determining whether the smallest set of vertices that
includes all shortest path connections between its elements is equal to $S$. It has
been established that this recognition problem is NP-complete when trying to find the
minimum number of steps required for a team of agents to visit every node in a graph
by moving along shortest paths between nodes. We have discovered that certain graph
categories allow for efficient resolution of this recognition problem, specifically
related to trees and specific types of trees known as star-free trees. Our solution
method for general trees can also be applied to other graph types, and we have
developed a particular approach for graphs with a limited diameter. Our algorithm for
this approach runs in $O(\Delta^2 n^2)$ time, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum
number of connections allowed between nodes and $n$ represents the total number of
nodes in the graph.

Imitation learning is known for reducing the number of trials required compared to traditional model-free reinforcement learning, but it can slow down learning due to limited expert demonstrations, particularly when the expert's actions are suboptimal. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel algorithm called TRAIL. By integrating planning into imitation learning, TRAIL utilizes value learning and priority retrieval to enable targeted expert demonstration analysis and efficient multi-step planning. As a result, TRAIL can significantly decrease the number of trials required and produce better policies by combining efficient expert demonstration usage with advanced planning capabilities. We validate the effectiveness of TRAIL over state-of-the-art imitation learning methods in a wide range of scenarios on the HackerWorld navigation dataset, demonstrating substantial improvements in efficient expert demonstration usage and the potential for enhanced performance through planning in complex environments.

Experts who collaborate on complex tasks can naturally teach each other through observation, a form of learning called Co-Imitation. Building on this concept, our team developed a collaborative algorithm that allows agents to observe and collaborate on the same complex task. Through experimentation in GridWorld environments with complex demonstrations that consisted of multiple sub-tasks, our results showed that the proposed Co-Imitation learning method required significantly fewer expert demonstrations (up to 80% fewer) to match the performance of experts, compared to standard Imitation Learning where experts provide direct demonstrations.

In this study, we examine how a sequential decoder using the polarized cutoff rate as its bias value performs, specifically looking at the decoding error probability in terms of the code block length. By employing a novel analysis based on the random walk theory, we are able to derive the decoding error probability for the sequential decoder. Additionally, we compare our findings with an alternative analysis method. As a result, we observe that when the bias value is set to the polarized cutoff rate, the decoding error probability exhibits a distinct pattern: it converges to a constant when the channel quality is below the cutoff rate and converges to zero when the channel quality exceeds the cutoff rate, both scenarios occurring as the code length increases.

Reformulation of the translation objective as a reduction in sequence similarity offers new insights and provides an alternative perspective on sequence-to-sequence tasks. This approach yields promising results when applied to translation using self-attention models trained through self-supervision. Our experiments demonstrate that the attention actions learned by these models can be effectively optimized, resulting in models with reduced action dimensions that perform better than the original and even surpass pre-trained models under certain conditions. Not only do these optimized action models outperform standard reinforcement learning approaches for translation, they also exhibit superior translation capabilities compared to the baseline models, providing a novel framework for analyzing and developing translation architectures.

This research addresses a critical challenge in designing and optimizing flexible end-effectors for rehabilitation robots - end-effector pose estimation during user interaction. To enhance accuracy and comfort, real-time monitoring of the end-effector's position relative to the patient is crucial. However, traditional methods that rely on distance measurements from the patient are prone to errors. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach using depth camera data, which provides precise spatial positioning of the end-effector in real-time. Furthermore, we integrate our approach with an extended Kalman filter to smoothly update position readings and minimize measurement noise. A comprehensive experimental approach and comprehensive user studies validate the effectiveness and accuracy of our proposed method and framework.

This article introduces the notion of continuous maps between QFS-spaces in relation to non-interference in program analysis, where a map is defined as continuous if pre-composing it with a sub-space inclusion results in equivalent output relations. A definition of continuous maps between QFS-spaces has been devised, and the following properties are proven: continuous maps form a structure similar to QFS-spaces and the concept of continuous maps aligns with that of non-interfering maps. Additionally, the ability to identify continuous sub-groups within the set of functions from QFS-space A to QFS-space B is demonstrated, specifically focusing on the relationship between continuous sub-groups and pairs of security labels.

The extent of polarization present within web content is amplified by the website's hyperlink structure, a factor to which users are also vulnerable. Besides, users' browsing behaviors contribute independently to this polarization. To understand this phenomenon, we analyzed the anonymity of hyperlinks through the anonymity of web users. Drawing on graph theory and privacy concepts, we developed a framework that quantifies the degree of users' exposure to controversial content beyond what they intentionally reveal. As an example, we examined the distribution of political views within web pages connected to the San Francisco Democratic District. Here, a significant disparity in political ideology was observed within web pages owned by owners of more conservative neighboring pages.

We prove that the Thompson group W_r contains a subgroup isomorphic to a given deterministic context-free language L, given L is defined by a deterministic pushdown automaton with a fixed state, provided the associated monoid has a finite congruence.

We propose using a monitor to measure both an open system and its environment, enabling bidirectional information exchange between them. This approach creates a unified framework that incorporates diverse models, such as unitary monitoring models and random circuit models. Our model shows that complex effects like the reversal of information flow and the involvement of the environment in these processes can be modeled within a single theoretical framework.

We are interested in classifying biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean ambient space that have a non-zero mean curvature vector, for the case when their tangent submanifold is compact and possesses a specific geometric property. This analysis is conducted within a specific class of submanifolds defined by a particular operator that includes well-known operators such as the shape operator and Jacobi field operator, within the context of Euclidean space. Our main objective is to establish a general framework and derive specific results for biharmonic hypersurfaces within a related geometric context, including a particular type of immersion into Euclidean space, within the context of compact tangent submanifolds. This framework will then be applied to specific operator contexts to obtain more targeted results. As part of this framework, we define a particular operator that generalizes two previously studied operators that relate to minimal submanifolds, within the context of Euclidean ambient space. This operator that we introduce will help us establish a broader framework and derive specific results for biharmonic submanifoles within a particular geometric context, including a particular type of immersion into Euclidean space, within the context of compact tangent submanifolds. This operator that we introduce will help us establish a more general framework and obtain specific results for biharmonic submanifoles within a particular geometric context, including a particular type of immersion into Euclidean space, within the context of compact tangent submanifolds. This operator that we introduce will help us

Let (N_p/q)^d denote the set of d-tuples composed of p/q-integer numbers. A notable example of such numbers is the p-adic integer. This work extends a previous study which characterised p/q-recognisable sets within the single-number set (N_p/q). It provides the set-based characterisation of p/q-recognisable subsets within the n-dimensional number set (N_p/q)^d.

We examine two possibilities within the $a_u$MSM model: if it can resolve the discrepancy of $\nu_e$ oscillation observed on Earth, and if it has a stability extension for the electroweak vacuum beyond its current understanding.

The LAMOST time-domain survey has detected over one million variable stars, yet many of them remain unexplored. The rapid classification of these objects is crucial, as their behavior may change on different timescales. The LAMOST collaboration has developed an efficient method, combining machine learning with human input, to categorize these variables quickly. This includes setting up a challenge where researchers can test and refine the algorithm. As a reward, all participants received free browsing of the LAMOST variable stars database. People voted on the best approach and it turned out that a simplified version of the method worked better. Furthermore, a new set of events, called the LAMOST transient catalog, has been put together from the data. It lists around 1400 potential transients that were detected during the survey and could be candidates for transient sources. This catalog is further explained along with the criteria used to identify them. Some of these sources, later reviewed, were found to be of different nature, from actual transients to variables and even binary sources. Additionally, an update to the known sources was made and some new discoveries were reported, including a potential tidal disruption and an extra event that could be associated with an already known source.

Convolutional Neural Networks are commonly used for their power to analyze images, but their application to image segmentation is hindered by a lack of encoder-decoder connections. A novel EG-CNN network has been proposed, incorporating a unique edge-gate module that enables the precise extraction of boundary information from intermediate features. This IEBI can be used to guide the segmentation process by identifying regions with high-magnitude values near the object's perimeter. As a result, the EG-CNN network enhances the original CNN by not only improving the accuracy of the segmentation but also the smoothness of the produced masks through a combination of conventional loss functions and a guidance loss. The proposed network's performance has been validated through extensive experiments on multiple datasets, demonstrating its superiority to current state-of-the-art EG-CNN models.

We have analyzed the concurrency control mechanisms used in MongoDB and other
collocated CloudMongo deployments, which have become increasingly popular and
essential for a wide range of applications. Our study shows that these systems
ensure the Serializability and Read Committed isolation levels for reads without
conflicting writes, similar to other NoSQL databases. For other isolated
read operations, we found two alternative definitions of snapshot isolation
that are consistent with WIREDTIGER's and CLUSTER's behavior. These definitions
are at least as strict as the standard read-committed isolation and may even
match committed read isolation for specific workloads. Our findings suggest that
comparing committed write timestamps with the read operation's start timestamp is
insufficient to prevent inconsistent isolated reads, particularly when considering
membrane theory. As a result, reading arbitrary data based on conflicting write
timestamps during read operations is likely necessary to achieve inconsistent
isolated reads. To make it easier for developers to create reliable applications
on top of non-deterministic concurrency control systems, we have also proposed a
new programming model called the Concurrent Execution Assumption, which allows for
deterministic program behavior regardless of the concurrency control system used.
This model has been the foundation for the design of several programming
languages and could provide a practical solution to a common issue faced by
MongoDB and other CloudMongo users, which is the occurrence of infinite loops in
their programs due to non-deterministic data values during

We establish that certain $e$-positivity properties observed in the $x \to -1$ specialization of certain functions, denoted as $f_{D}(x)$, hold for the full functions $f_{D}(x)$ themselves, when considering specific paths $D$ with long descends. This discovery expands upon previous $e$-positivity findings by S. Choi for specific cases, such as the "twisted Macdonald polynomials" and "rational Catalan functions". This paper also explores $e$-positivity properties for specific subcases with long descends, including those with long rises.

When learning from attended information, an agent must decide which entities to focus on. 
In an ideal scenario, it would be able to minimize prediction error at all previously attended moments. 
However, due to limited computational power, this goal is unattainable. 
We hypothesize that using "hindsight summaries" could enable the system to minimize attended prediction error more effectively. 
These summaries, drawn from the full historical data, serve as proxies for the actual experiences and guide the system's future attention by seemingly unrelated criteria. 
To test this hypothesis, we applied a variation of the Relevance Weighted Passive Aggressive algorithm to artificial reaction time data. 
In this setup, each system attempt to solve a math problem either succeeds or fails, and attention is directed to previously failed attempts only. 
Due to the specificity of attention, these moments go to the core of actually focusing on the most critically solved problems. 
However, by weighting these moments against a "hindsight summary" of all attempted problems (based on their complex feature structures), 
the system is able to minimize prediction error at all previously attended moments with significantly higher accuracy - minuscule compared to the original error. 
This provides a plausible explanation for how attention, which seems unrelated to prediction error, could be functionally adapted to focus on the most crucial moments with purpose.

In medical image analysis, it's essential for models to function reliably and avoid perpetuating implicit biases present in the data. While techniques exist to reduce bias, they often increase computational costs during training. A novel method, implicit bias regularization (iBR), has been introduced to achieve bias reduction directly from the image patches, without the need for protected group labels. The proposed method aims to minimize group discrimination without compromising accuracy. The proposed method introduces a novel approach to measure implicit bias and proposes the 'uniform bias' concept. Experimental results in medical skin lesion classification demonstrate that iBR can reduce implicit biases while maintaining accuracy. The proposed method achieves comparable performance to existing bias-reduction techniques but with significantly lower computational costs, outperforming other methods in both accuracy and bias reduction.

We examine the magnetic properties of Ising models as they go through periodic changes in temperature and external magnetic fields. This study focuses on two combinations: first, where magnetic spin interactions occur in groups of three within an arbitrary network structure, and second, on a fully connected network where varying magnetic spin interactions are investigated. On any network structure without cycles, the previous findings confirm that the hysteresis effect disappears, giving rise to a unique equilibrium state and loss of magnetization memory. In contrast, combinations that include the mentioned triangular network and the complete network demonstrate significant and diverse hysteresis behavior. This indicates that the origin of hysteresis is determined not simply by the network's overall properties, but rather, where local interactions are taken into account.

Researchers have developed a comprehensive understanding of how solar energetic particles are formed through the use of novel models. These models integrated data from various solar heliospheric platforms to determine the energy distribution of particles at a specific location near the solar surface. A key concept proposed was that the observed energy distribution of protons could be explained by two main factors: thermal processes and non-thermal shocks. A significant concept was that the ratio of these factors could vary depending on heliocentric distance. Data from multiple cases of solar energetic particle events supported this idea. At very close distances from the sun, the data showed a different pattern compared to what was observed at one astronomical unit. The energy distribution data suggested a different mechanism at play, with a higher percentage of high-energy protons compared to one astronomical unit. However, it's important to note that this concept could not be applied to all solar events and was primarily found in strong shock events and those with specific characteristics.

A significant challenge in Continuous Learning arises from the need to know what new categories to look for. This study introduces an attention-based neural network model that can automatically detect new emotion categories through the use of self-relevant new features. This model focuses on a specific application for recognizing emotions from text but its design can be applied to other tasks and modalities. The model is tested on multiple datasets with different languages and demonstrates a significant increase in accuracy for recognizing various emotions, particularly surprise, compared to traditional methods. The attention-based neural network model uses quadratic programming to balance the benefits of discovering new categories with maintaining performance on existing categories. Notably, it can perform continuous learning without needing to revisit previous data, addressing a common issue in deep learning models.

Research on the effects of hydrostatic pressure up to 12.3 GPa on Bi5FeTi3O15 under temperature conditions of 300 K, 423 K, and 573 K has been conducted using X-ray diffraction and differential thermal analysis. Initial findings from DTA showed no significant changes up to 8.54 GPa at 300 K, 423 K, and 573 K, while XRD patterns remained consistent with the Bi5(fee) structure. As pressure increased beyond 8.54 GPa at 300 K, 423 K, and 573 K, XRD displayed features matching the Bi5(orth) structure, indicating a phase transition. Utilizing the Le Bail and Pawletta methods, lattice parameters were determined for both phases. In the Bi5(fee) phase, lattice parameters 'a' and 'c' decreased linearly with pressure, while in the Bi5(orth) phase, all lattice parameters exhibited a similar decrease of approximately 2.4 GPa^-1. The bulk modulus values were calculated as 82.6 ± 4.2 GPa, 84.6 ± 4.2 GPa, and 86.6 ± 4.2 GPa at 300 K, 423 K, and 573 K,

This research explores the utilization of risk-sensitive optimal control in solving complex navigation problems for vehicles and nautical crafts operating in crowded environments. By integrating the theory of control risk with time-dilated paths, the authors demonstrate that these discrete paths remain within a certain error margin compared to the best possible trajectories. A key factor in this bound is localized, which significantly reduces inaccuracies in areas without other vehicles or ships. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm is proposed for finding nearly optimal paths, and its effectiveness is illustrated through practical applications and testing simulations.

If we consider any initial conditions in the Euler equations that are smooth away from the origin and have a strong shock wave forming, it has been proven that if certain values of adiabatic power exceed a critical threshold, a smooth cavity will form at a critical time. This finding can be seen as a restatement of Lax's cavity expansion theorem but with a more general context, and it also reveals that the cavity formation time is sensitive to slight variations in initial conditions, particularly when the adiabatic power is near the critical value.

The interpretation of $B \to \pi \ell \nu$ decay rates in terms of form factors can be replaced by a set of universal functions that depend on a variable 's', with two frameworks - Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed - offering distinct parameterizations. This study investigates the impact of choosing one framework over the other on the inferred values of form factors. The impact is found to be more significant at the edges of the allowed region than in the middle. A mapping between the two sets of functions is also proposed to translate form factor results from one framework to the other.

A class of exactly solvable SUSY quantum potential models in one dimension, characterized by the polynomial Heisenberg algebra, is shown to encompass the harmonic oscillator as a special case and through unitary transformation to another category of non-singular potential models in one dimension.

The study addresses a general class of maps on R^n that include C^1 locally finite-growth maps. It involves analyzing a specific set in R^n under these maps, where the map's coercivity and nonrepelling behavior of infinity are required. The central issue is determining an appropriate definition of Lyapunov exponent for points outside this set, given the map's specific properties. The experimentally observed average exponent of a related, highly growth-map-conjugated system is used as an example to support the feasibility of the proposed concept. The proposed framework allows for a broad range of maps and sets, provided they conform to specified behavior at infinity. The approach also facilitates the study of asymptotically nonrepelling boundaries in contexts such as rational dynamics and polynomial-like maps.

Research into hybrid quantum circuits has been advancing quickly, with Josephson applications showing promising signs for quantum computing and ultra-sensitive detectors in single and mesoscopic circuits. A critical area of study is how these circuits switch from a zero-voltage state to a finite-voltage state in single and mesoscopic Josephson devices, with another key question being the effect of phase locking between Josephson junctions in an asymmetric SQUID loop on the switching current compared to a single junction. A simulation conducted on an asymmetric Al/AlOx/Al Josephson SQUID loop with specific material properties and dimensions, demonstrates the effectiveness of a simulation approach using the Anderson orthogonality catastrophe concept to model the Anderson charge stagnation and the Anderson stasis of kinetic energy in the loop. This approach is shown to result in a significantly larger critical charge and critical energy in both single and mesoscopic cases, with the Anderson charges and energies becoming trapped in Anderson wells, ultimately affecting the critical charge and energy due to sufficient energy dissipation. A Josephson phase-locking model is also presented that combines these model components with the Anderson currents and voltages, with the simulation capable of reproducing characteristic features of hybrid quantum devices, with the Anderson charges and energies playing a significant role in the switching process from a zero-voltage state to a finite-voltage state. A model using this approach is also presented that results in bi-stable Anderson well states, with possible implications for using hybrid quantum circuits as the basis for persistent memory

Building on initial insights, we obtain closed-form expressions for the non-abelian aether term, specifically the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, the trace anomaly, and various Casimir energies for gluons in confined channels. Notably, the non-abelian aether term yields universal expressions for both the trace anomaly and Casimir energies of gluons within certain bounded geometries. An examination of large $N_c$ limits reveals that the non-abelian aether term scales as $N_c^2$ and remains consistent with derivations based on path integral methods, also confirming the equality of energy density and pressure in Casimir scenarios.

This paper explores the challenges of hedging HFT portfolios, focusing on the difficulty of calculating expected liquidity costs due to the interplay between the portfolio value and order book dynamics. Although a precise model-based approach yields an intricate integral that's computationally difficult to solve, a simplified quadratic approximation provides a clearer calculation of anticipated liquidity costs pre-hedging. Comparisons with Monte Carlo simulations confirm the accuracy of this approximated formula. Nonetheless, a broader implication emerges: calculating expected losses for high-frequency hedging strategies involves an intransitive relationship, favoring either higher frequencies with minimal hedging costs or lower frequencies paired with substantial costs.

This work seeks to examine how variational principles associated with complex, heterogeneous materials can be used to understand, including the study of integral functions subject to differentiation rules, despite their inherent lack of continuity, despite the prevailing absence of continuity.

We studied the properties of tidal structures found in early-stage galaxies using data from the HST/ACS and the SHAPES survey. Our analysis focused on understanding how often these tidal formations appear, their characteristics in relation to the main body of the galaxy, and how often they are losing mass due to interactions with the main galaxy. Our findings show that as the main galaxy becomes more massive, the frequency of these tidal formations decreases, from around 30 percent in low-mass galaxies to approximately 10 percent in more massive ones. There isn't as significant of a relationship between tidal structures and galaxy mass when looking at the most massive galaxies only. Our results also show that the mass of these tidal structures is comparable to that of small satellite galaxies that have already merged with the main galaxy. Based on this, we propose that the mass distribution observed around galaxies the mass of the Milky Way might not entirely reflect the total number of these smaller companions in the local universe.

Distributing chances for future success within a society defines our initial conditions, which ripple through to subsequent generations. Our intertemporal framework for stochastic transitions highlights how granting opportunities to less privileged individuals not only boosts their chances of succeeding but also improves future generations' prospects. This concept is modeled using an intricate probability matrix that incorporates various possible outcomes and represents different societal structures. This framework is then applied to explore the dynamics of allocating opportunities in different societal contexts, which aligns with findings from empirical studies but also extends to theoretical scenarios. These studies reveal that different allocation strategies can lead to significantly different results across multiple generations. For some societal structures, those favoring equal distribution may not produce the optimal long-term benefits. However, these results also indicate that different structures might require different allocation methods to maximize opportunities for present and future generations, which in turn suggests a need for sophisticated intertemporal welfare functions to make such decisions.

Developing and refining computer programs to simulate complex computer applications is a challenging task. It is particularly challenging to accurately model laser-based systems, including network configurations, that rely on numerical methods to solve a set of coupled differential equations that describe the behavior of a system. In this study, we introduce and discuss the advantages of using the discrete variable representation (DVR) method to simulate NLO-based systems and provide a detailed explanation of how to implement this technique, including the underlying mathematical principles such as numerical integration and the selection of appropriate DVR basis sets. By comparing the results of the simulations with available experimental data, we demonstrate that using the DVR method to model NLO-based systems yields accurate predictions that are consistent with observed data.
Linear dimension reduction at near-isometric levels is unfeasible for the ell_p unit ball when p differs from 2.

The beam-beam interaction causes a shift in working point and non-linear growth of beam size in the collider due to resonances. These effects can no longer be ignored with the increased beam intensity in the High-Luminosity LHC. It is crucial to account for the beam-beam interaction when choosing the correct non-linear optics that ensures good dynamic aperture and minimizes beam loss from resonance-driven scattering. Given the limited space for correctors at the interaction points, finding the right balance between corrector room and corrector performance has become a challenge. In this study, the impact of beam-beam interactions on the HL-LHC's dynamic aperture, beam size, and tail growth have been analyzed and the feasibility of compensating beam-shift with correctors near the interaction points has been explored. The approach used for this analysis involved a comprehensive model of the collider including correctors, closed orbit displacements at the interaction points, and random multipoles representing the effect of aperture-limited beam-beam fields. Findings from this study can be directly applied to the collider design studies for the HL-LHC.

This paper addresses a specific challenge in distributed optimization on networks, where malicious agents disrupt communication by broadcasting false information. We tackle this problem within a specific framework: asynchronous stochastic settings, where the network structure changes constantly, leading to varying communication patterns. Our goal is to develop an efficient, distributed algorithm that ensures safe convergence even in the presence of malicious agents. To achieve this, we propose a projection-based stochastic algorithm and, under the assumption of a strongly convex objective function, we provide a theoretical performance analysis. Notably, our approach does not require the network to be globally connected at any given time, and our convergence theory takes into account the cost of stochastic gradient calculations.

In the early stages of designing new cosmological instruments, a crucial step is to computationally emulate their observed data, which can then be used to anticipate their performance.  However, there are a variety of instrumental biases that need to be accounted for, each of which is unique to the specific instrument in use.  Although some of these biases are difficult to simulate, many can be effectively modeled with relatively simple algorithms, even if they are not perfectly faithful to real physical processes.  Given the computational efficiency of these simplified algorithms, even the slowest upcoming instruments would be capable of simulating the effects of at least some instrumental biases on their data.  As such, incorporating instrumental biases into the simulated data sets for projects like Simons Observatory and CMB-Sensei is now computationally feasible.  In this study, we present simplified models for several instrumental biases and utilize them to simulate the data that Simons Observatory and CMB-Sensei are expected to observe.  Specifically, we generate simulated data sets for Simons Observatory that incorporate a range of instrumental biases, including foreground asymmetries, dipole leaks, and polarization contamination, which are then reflected in the power spectra of the data.  In doing so, we have created a simulated data set for Simons Observatory that is perhaps the most comprehensive to date, and which can be used to anticipate the performance of the instrument and simulate its cosmic variance limited parameters of interest.  In addition, we have developed and utilized instrumental bias

Statistical parse generators utilize the same data to learn from and make predictions, with the task being that of linearizing a parse tree. These models have achieved high accuracy, yet a closer examination reveals significant disparities in performance on various task formulations. Our research explores whether the gap in performance between full tree linearization and a full tree structure is manageable, with results showing that BART exhibits a 13% discrepancy (0.56 F-score) and interestingly, the model performs better linearizing tree structures than constructing them.

Deepfake images continue to evolve in complexity while simultaneously introducing new challenges for creators who face difficulties in producing visually convincing forgeries. To address these challenges, we developed two innovative networks, CrossStitchLoa and CrossStitchGen, capable of accurately detecting deepfakes in multiple sources simultaneously and transferring training knowledge to unseen targets across multiple domains. Unlike conventional approaches that often focus on single-classification tasks, our networks must navigate the multi-classification problem across various image domains. To tackle this, we incorporated a cross-stitch cell design that allows network components to exchange information freely, facilitating both self-learning and inter-domain knowledge transfer. This flexible architecture enables network components to exchange information both within and between different domains. As a result, our method achieves superior performance by combining supraglacial and infraglacial processing layers. We validated the effectiveness of our approach on the WIDE and FaceForensics+ data sets through rigorous experimentation.

This paper analyzes the performance of regular LDPC codes in systems with erasures that are not uniformly distributed. Specifically, we derive new bounds for the maximum tolerable erasure probability during the threshold region. By adjusting an initial assumption, we improve these bounds and provide accurate estimation formulas for two types of LDPC codes – one related to the belief propagation algorithm and another specifically for regular LDPC codes with chordal structures. These formulas can be used as effective tools to study complex irregular LDPC codes. To validate the effectiveness of our methodology, we apply it to a specific TCP LDPC code used in the 5G standard, and the results demonstrate its efficiency.

We investigated the security of vacuum+weak decoy state quantum key distribution (QKD) and found that, despite not having access to the weak decoy states, eavesdroppers can insert and monitor all sent photons, effectively controlling the QKD system. Even if the QKD protocol uses an infinite number of weak decoy states, enabling precise statistical analysis, Vussier's attack poses a significant threat. Furthermore, we demonstrated that combining two different weak decoy states does not prevent success. Nevertheless, our research suggests that incorporating strong decoy states can achieve secure vacuum+decoy state QKD and that the security issue arises primarily from the feasibility of inserting and monitoring all photons, which is unique to photon source-based QKD systems and does not apply to other QKD implementations using weak decoy states.

AsFacilities for edge computing are geographically distributed, their combined location significantly influences total energy usage.  Our model identifies optimal edge computing facility locations to minimize overall energy consumption, taking into account the energy required for computing and faciliites.  We propose two strategies to resolve this location-selection problem, which can be applied to networks of varying sizes.  Our simulation results demonstrate that our proposed strategies yield substantial reductions in energy consumption, and we observe a notable decrease in energy usage at distribution facilities.  Our findings also indicate that edge computing can lead to more balanced network loads, and we conclude that integrating edge computing into network design can result in significant overall energy savings.

This research focuses on angle function and its application to isometric embeddability problems. Angle function was initially defined in strictly convex Euclidean space and later researched in more general convex space before its definition was expanded to non-strictly convex space. This study explores angle function within the context of finite-dimensional normed space and examines its potential to resolve conformal embeddability questions. Specifically, we establish a relationship between angle function and the conformal embeddability of a manifold into normed space and provide a method for checking conformal embeddability through this relationship. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a given sphere in Euclidean space cannot be isometrically embedded into $L_p$ space when $1 \lt p \lt 2$.

This article outlines a general approach to comparing Isomorphism classes of orders within number fields. The framework established can be applied to prior results concerning number fields and orders. A specific criterion is set for orders in number fields of a given rank, isomorphism types that exhibit identical properties. The framework also defines partial order relations between these isomorphism types based on invariants. A significant outcome is the demonstration of irreducibility in certain subgraphs formed within these order structures. Furthermore, a key bound is derived for the invariants used in these order relations. The methods described here are motivated by earlier work on countable partially ordered sets of isomorphism types of number fields and orders. The framework presented has been computationally verified for a wide range of small ranks, and some results are derived computationally without relying on deep theoretical insights. The algorithm described can be applied to count the number of isomorphism types within a specified range of invariants, compare specific isomorphism types, and study order structures among isomorphism types. The algorithm employed in this work includes contributions from previous studies on counting and comparing number fields, as well as innovations in order counting and comparison. The framework presented in this work is partly constructed to facilitate these computational outcomes. The results obtained in this work are partly constructed to aid these computational outcomes.

The resolution of pressure influences the spread of a nitrogen jet as it interacts with a surface, with changes in backpressure significantly impacting jet characteristics including velocity, spread, and the presence of vortical structures. Increasing backpressure causes a transition in jet behavior from coaxial to spiral, which has implications for understanding high pressure nitrogen jets used in industrial applications such as sandblasting and jet engraving. Researchers examined how surface entrapment of jets affects their behavior at varying backpressures (4.5 to 20 bar) and initial pressures (30 to 60 bar) using Laser-Induced Fluorescence and schlieren imaging techniques.

In a young planetary system, the emergence of planetesimals from the dissipative flow of a protoplanetary disk is believed to be influenced by self-maintaining swirling currents, or vortices. These vortices can create conditions where dust concentrations become so high that they collapse under their own gravity. To understand how long these critical conditions can be maintained, a timeline was established comparing the timescales of several key processes: the creation of initial vortices, their destruction by a collapsing structure, their replication through collapse, their replication through streaming influences, and the growth of resulting planetary bodies. Computational models show that self-maintaining vortices can be formed and that they can be kept within stable limits by balancing their growth and external forces. This discovery provides a robust framework for further investigations into the formation of planetary systems, as it allows for the incorporation of additional factors such as streaming influences and external pressures.

We develop a detection method for neutral modes that persists in the presence of disorder. The protocol is effective at identifying charge-neutral current carriers in insulating systems with symmetry, regardless of their behavior--whether they exhibit semi-metallic, quantum Hall, or other characteristics. The detection method is adaptable to various types of symmetries, including magnetic, particle-hole, and chiral symmetries, and can be used to distinguish between carriers with different dispersion behaviors. The proposed method is highly versatile, applicable not only to quantum Hall systems but also to Weyl, Dirac, and nodal-line semimetals. In a quantitative study using time-evolution under a sudden change of Hamiltonian, we find that the method yields robust results when the initial wave function is an eigenstate of the disorder-free Hamiltonian, providing an explanation for the observed performance in previous experiments under ideal conditions.

We demonstrate that the quantum group U_q(g) associated with a simple Lie algebra g possesses a structured basis, derived from a set of quantum group generators introduced by Brzezi\'nski and Dascalescu. This basis aligns with the action of the braid group, as described by Lusztig, and maintains compatibility with the simple reflections and Dynkin automorphisms on the Borel basis of the quantum group.

To address challenges in decentralized learning for massive MIMO systems with limited bandwidth, this study proposes a reduced-decision-scale decentralized gradient descent algorithm. By combining local gradient updates with periodic global consensus updates, the proposed method balances efficient adaptation and accurate convergence. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the algorithm's performance improves at a rate of $O(\max\{\frac{1}{T},\tau\})$, where $T$ represents the total number of iterations, and $\tau$denotes the interval between consensus updates. Key findings include an inverse relationship with the number of decision dimensions and a direct relationship with the number of $K$ devices, which can be managed through localized learning and over-parameterization. Simulations using real-world datasets confirm the algorithm's superior spectral efficiency and sum-rate performance compared to existing methods.

The concept of a phase transition in hard-disk systems, which serves as a benchmark for studying phases with high entropy, has been viewed through a lens suggesting the hard-disk scenario may be more intricate than initially thought and requires further exploration. Our studies have faced significant challenges due to the intricate nature of cluster algorithms applicable to systems with rotational degrees of freedom and the lack of clear definitions for symmetry-breaking order parameters. Despite these obstacles, our Monte-Carlo simulations and molecular-dynamics-based cluster-algorithm modifications allow us to assert with confidence that what was once thought to be a first-order phase transition in hard-disk systems may actually be either continuously gradual or exhibit discontinuities, depending on the filling rate and likely does not involve any distinguishable symmetry-breaking.

This research investigates the impact of nuclear parton distribution functions on jet characteristics in the inelastic scattering of lepton-nucleus. We utilize the General Monte Carlo for parton level and PYTHIA 6.501 for jet formation. Our results indicate a jet structure function that scales with the number of produced particles, and we demonstrate that the effect of nuclear modifications propagates to the jet's substructure in the form of a scale-dependent convolution of the jet structure function and the modified parton distribution, consistent with the collinear factorization framework. Furthermore, we find that the nuclear modification factor influences the jet's inelastic profile in a linear manner. We also examine the dependence on the energy transferred during the interaction, the inelastic variable itself, the number of produced particles, transverse momentum, and the momentum fraction carried by the in-flight particle. We anticipate that J/$\psi$ production within jets can offer valuable insights into the modification of the parton distribution functions within the nucleus.

Pyramid schemes, characterized by their deceptive high returns, inevitably lead to substantial financial losses for the majority of participants. Analyzing nearly a year's worth of blockchain data from the cryptocurrency pyramid scheme Forsage allows researchers to study an unusually large number of participants who openly share personal information and transaction histories. Findings from this study reveal several key observations: around 99% of participants end up with negative returns; around 5% of participants manage to avoid losses by leaving the scheme early; and around 20% of participants lose more than $100 thousand. Additionally, the discovered exit strategies and time frames provide valuable insights for assessing the potential risks of other cryptocurrency pyramid schemes.

We have examined the age, metallicity and stellar population of the globular cluster candidate GCs in the Milky Way using the HRRD database. Through the use of the HRRD tool, we obtained individual parameters for individual stars within each of the 149 fields studied. By applying the isochrone fitting method with the LEVITAR code, we determined the global parameters for each of the 24 local globular clusters. The results show that the GCs share a wide range of ages, spanning from 3.6 to 12.7 billion years, as well as a diverse spectrum of metallicities, going from -1.59 to +0.42. The discovery of the newly identified WC2 has enabled researchers to generate a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the formation and evolution of the Milky Way.

The influence of the quark's mass on the parton level is considered in the process $q\bar{q} \to \gamma \gamma$ and calculated at order $m^2$, taking into account the quark's finite mass in the amplitude for this reaction. These calculations result in modifying the transverse momentum distribution of the photons, especially in the low mass range, where the effect of the quark's mass is most significant and influences the distribution up to $p_T^2 \sim m^2$. The effect of the quark's mass is also observed in the total cross section in a low-mass range, with the influence decreasing as the mass increases, at order $m^4$. The calculation of the process is carried out in the framework of the Standard Model, with the reaction occurring in the region where the invariant mass of the photons is much greater than the quark's mass, with the relevant heavy quark being either the bottom or charm quark.

Researchers have long utilized tight-binding (TB) models to efficiently simulate and describe materials' interactions with light. The TB method is versatile and can be seamlessly integrated with first-principles principles to generate accurate models that retain atomic-level detail. The method's simplicity and visualization capabilities make it an ideal tool for initial analysis of light-matter interactions, however the standard velocity gauge implementation has limitations. To improve its accuracy, the study introduces a new approach based on the length gauge that utilizes position-momentum operators to properly account for the coupling between electrons and incoming photons. This approach can be easily applied to existing nonhermitean TB models and provides better results than the velocity gauge for these types of models. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by comparing its results with first-principles calculations and showing its advantages over the velocity gauge in certain regimes. The new formula for the dielectric function derived from this approach can be applied to both infinite slabs and finite geometries and offers more accurate results for cases where the velocity gauge approach fails. To improve the accuracy of the velocity gauge approach, a correction formula is introduced that can be applied to both infinite slabs and finite geometries.

A generic tensor network can serve as a robust error correction code by creating a relationship between its underlying geometry and the physical system it represents. However, if the network is composed of a singular tensor type and functions as a corrector, significant limitations are imposed on the network. A notable class of such networks can be characterized as "1-coupled" systems. A key feature of these clusters is their ability to be analyzed using a method known as the 1-coupling operation, which is often associated with the fusion rules in topological theories. Our study identifies a set of rules that any cluster-based code must adhere to, and it is argued that the described cluster-defining operations are among the most fundamental principles in the field of quantum error correction.

We've developed an efficient method to evaluate the impact of structural changes on a quantum yield in systems where light leads to a stable, small population of photo-products. Focusing on conical intersections and photo-isomerization in retinal as examples, we discovered that a minimal distortion to the system can have a significant impact. This sensitivity to structural changes at conical intersections is crucial for condensed-phase photochemistry and biological light-sensing. Furthermore, our approach can also examine the effect of perturbations resulting from light itself. Our formulas for the sensitivity to both structural and optical disturbances are derived based on the properties of photo-equilibrium.

As businesses rely more on digital tools, they generate vast amounts of data, 
which can be utilized to create predictive models for process optimization. 
These models vary in complexity, with some using statistical calculations to 
intermediate results, while others use machine learning to forecast process 
outcomes. 
However, there is a lack of studies using real process data to evaluate and 
cluster processes based on characteristics relevant to optimization, 
especially in the financial sector. 
Building on the available process mining tools, we use complete process 
mining traces to develop a novel feature set and apply clustering algorithms 
to a comprehensive process dataset from the public sector. 
Our results indicate that processes can be effectively grouped, with each group 
requiring a tailored optimization approach. 
Moreover, our developed model achieves a high degree of accuracy in 
predicting process outcomes, including cycle times and completion rates, 
with predicted actual correlations exceeding 0.75 for different processes. 
Our research suggests the importance of creating multiple models to capture 
process variations and delivering tailored predictions, which can be applied to 
process features, mining traces, and outcomes.

Public sentiment analysis via social media has the potential to significantly
improve our comprehension of the effects of natural disasters. The way this
comprehension can be enhanced is by leveraging pre-trained models that have
been specifically trained on a variety of domains through a single-domain
adaptation process. This paper makes the following contributions in this process:
- It gathers approximately 100,000 tweets related to the magnitude and
impact of the earthquake that struck Southern Turkey and Syria on June 7, 2023;
- It develops a novel technique for categorizing tweets based on their
descriptive content;
- It establishes a meaningful correlation between our proposed
earthquake classification and the Geolcst taxonomy;
- It demonstrates a unique domain adaptation approach and achieves a notable
increase in classification accuracy of 7% compared to training a model exclusively
on labeled data.

This paper provides detailed descriptions of several Gelfand-Shilov spaces by examining their Fourier transforms and establishing specific growth conditions. Notably, it offers innovative characterizations of these spaces without utilizing exponential bounds by analyzing the decay of Fourier transforms. The Fourier transforms define continuous operators among certain Strichartz spaces, and this is achieved by demonstrating that they map functions into appropriate Gaussian-related spaces. As a result, new and revised criteria are established for functions whose Fourier transforms belong to these spaces. The article also explores the interrelationships between these specific Gelfand-Shilov spaces and examine their norms by investigating how they relate to each other. The proof of the continuity of the Fourier transform is based on a key property of these spaces that arises from closure under composition. Additionally, this work extends previous results about the closure of these spaces under composition and the study of paraconvolving functions.

We analyzed changes in the Hα line, optical and far-ultraviolet continuum during 13 Hα line events at the Sunspot 2441. This is a large, complex active region that underwent an X8.2 class X-ray flare on 2017 September 06. Three minor X88 flare events followed within 48 hours. Each event consisted of multiple optical, Hα line and continuum flare episodes. There was a strong correlation between the line broadening and the continuum flux in the UV and optical. The continuum during the flare showed a distinct double-peaked pattern in the UV. The initial UV continuum was driven by a massive flare eruption, while the ongoing UV continuum was supplied by a massive flare loop. The continuum during the line broadening was dominated by dense and cool plasma. The continuum during the continuum flare was supplied by hot and less dense plasma. For the line broadening events, the UV continuum was located at temperatures below 10^5 K, which is consistent with the emission from dense and cool plasma in the lower atmosphere. The continuum during the continuum flare was located at temperatures above 10^5 K, which is consistent with the emission from hot plasma in the loop plasma. The continuum during the continuum flare was 1.5 times greater than the line broadening events, which is consistent with the continuum during the continuum flare being supplied by a massive flare loop. The continuum during the continuum flare lasted for

This study uses linearized Sanitation Equation to analyze one-dimensional wave propagation in a single-unit system with non-Hermitian properties. We are examining light propagation within a porous media structure that contains two optical cavities. These cavities utilize a unique mechanism for transferring and redirecting fluid and light. By applying a Floquet-Bloch approach, we developed analytical models to study how energy moves within this structure. Our results show that in a PT symmetric phase, waves can travel through the unit cell, while in a PT broken phase, they become trapped within the cell and dissipate. Additionally, we found that in both phases of the PT symmetry, broken phase specifically, non-reciprocal behavior can be achieved. Our theoretical predictions are supported by experimental data obtained from our setup.

This study explores the application of a dynamical cavity method to a specific type of Boolean network known as the Kauffman model. These networks are characterized by multiple inputs that influence each node through various types of self-interactions. We developed an approach that allows us to calculate higher-order moments within a cavity framework, expanding on previous cavity methods limited to capturing only basic moment statistics. This extension to the dynamical setting enables us to model the evolution of complex patterns of coactivation among network units. However, it's essential to note that the dynamical cavity method may struggle with scenarios involving extensive clusters of mutually activated network units.

Quantum mechanics calculations for calcium-48 and lead-208 demonstrate that using a coarse atomic nucleus grid increases the restoration of isospin symmetry. Based on the NC30 and ARIEL2 experiments at CRAQ, which involved the atomic nucleus calcium-48 and calculated the restoration of isospin symmetry, this concept can also be applied to heavy nuclear systems. The NC30 and ARIEL2 datasets were utilized to calculate the isospin charge distribution for the $^ {40}$Ca$^{13+}$ ion and found evidence of enhanced symmetry restoration within the atomic nucleus due to quantum effects, with calculated values of $\langle T_z\rangle = 0.5\pm 0.1$ in agreement with previous measurements. Furthermore, this principle may be applicable to heavy nuclear targets, potentially increasing the observed symmetry restoration.

Deep neural networks classified point clouds have a low certified accuracy when it comes to withstanding twisting transformations. A new framework called TPC has been proposed to address this issue. The TPC framework expands upon existing research by considering both neural network and total energy loss functions when calculating the certified accuracy.
