A key benefit of using the TPC framework is that it allows for greater flexibility in applying various optimization methods to calculate the highest certified accuracy. A sub-optimal strategy called TC-PC was also proposed as an alternative to make the training process differentiable and achieve higher certified accuracy. Experimental results show that both strategies within the TPC framework outperform existing methods and achieve up to a 20.5% increase in certified accuracy.

Continuous wave radar systems with frequency modulation (FMCW) are highly regarded for their ability to detect motion and distance simultaneously. Leveraging the advantage of wideband communication, radar systems can achieve improved range resolution and signal-to-noise ratios. Nonetheless, when multiple FMCW radar systems operate in proximity, the risk of mutual interference increases, potentially compromising detection accuracy. We address this challenge by developing adaptive chirp design schemes that adapt to each FMCW radar system's individual needs. Our research explores two key performance metrics: interference probabilities and system throughput. We present an efficient algorithm based on a neural network that enables real-time adaptation of chirps per packet, demonstrating significant improvements in_few_packet_scenarios._Our_algorithm'_flexibility_allows_for_adoption_by_commercial_radar_systems,_which can enhance their performance by dynamically optimizing performance. Moreover, generalizing our results highlights the advantages of adaptive FMCW protocols over traditional approaches.

Our work delves into our modeling of cycles within our proposed cycle-aware
time-encoding method for learning temporal patterns in knowledge graphs.
Furthermore, our work explores the integration of embedding learning within
our proposed SCAT model. Also, our work explores parameter optimization via
Lars and shows how it can be applied to our model.

Using a specific potential, the Shell Model method was employed to investigate the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. To enhance accuracy, this study integrates many-body corrections into the Shell Model framework, allowing for a precise assessment of correlation effects within a 2p-h excitation framework. By comparing results within this narrower excitation framework to those found by three-body Force in the full valence space, correlation contributions are comparable in magnitude to nuclear potential parameters. Notably, SHM and three-body Force yield nearly identical resonance frequencies and strengths, whereas SHM exhibits a slight shift in the high-energy tail due to the absence of specific three-body configurations present in the full valence space.

Nonlinear dynamical systems underpin many natural phenomena and are essential
to understanding complex systems across various disciplines. To facilitate
their analysis and interpretation, the Koopman operator framework enables the
development of data-driven models by leveraging existing measurements. Although
existing frameworks effectively handle linear systems and their applications,
nonlinear systems demand more adaptable approaches. This study proposes a unified
framework that integrates the Fréchet derivative and the Bochner integral to
extend the Koopman operator to nonlinear dynamical systems. This new approach
yields a set of properties and relationships mirroring those of linear systems,
and it can be applied to infinite-dimensional parabolic partial differential
equations. Furthermore, a discrete spectral representation is derived using
kernel methods, facilitating efficient computation. The computational
efficiency of this method can be enhanced by drawing on techniques from the
classical Koopman framework. Empirical results validate the theoretical
findings and illustrate the operator's application to a heat equation and
advection-diffusion equation. The reformulated Koopman operator offers a robust
tool for analyzing and interpreting nonlinear dynamical systems.

Neural text generation models often struggle to capture a sentence's main idea due to a lack of efficient sentence-level representation. To address this challenge, we propose SparseGAN, a technique that leverages attention-sparsened decoding to create multiple parallel generation paths and efficiently represents sentences. By selecting and merging word-level features with the path-level features, we enable the generator to capture a more comprehensive sentence representation while enhancing diversity and reducing repetitive generated words. Experimental results on standard text generation benchmarks demonstrate that SparseGAN improves representation quality, leading to enhanced generation performance.

To explore interstellar panspermia, we've established key requirements for a viable microcosmic life form in various stellar environments. Our analysis focuses on three settings: massive stars, binary star systems, and exoplanetary systems within the Milky Way. We found that, due to their extremely high temperatures and surrounding environments, none of the first two settings could potentially accommodate interstellar panspermia. However, certain types of binary star systems, such as uncontactable and comfortably distant ones, along with certain exoplanets, including surface habitable zones and ocean worlds, could potentially carry interstellar panspermia. To explore this possibility, we've outlined necessary conditions and examples of suitable exoplanets in the Kennedy and Trappist star systems.

We investigate the biases introduced by incomplete foreground removal in Cosmic Microwave Map components when estimating B-mode parameters, using simulated data from the Simons Observatory and their planned foreground removal processes. Although FIRM and SIMBA generally perform well in minimizing noise, our results show that the foreground removal methods can lead to significant errors in parameter estimation beyond the statistical uncertainty for significant signals ($>10^{-7}$ for $r$ and $10^{-27}$ for $A_{LH}$). Specifically, we found that the parameter estimation lies outside its $1\sigma$ confidence interval in such cases. The degree of bias introduced by the methods varies with $A_{LH}$'s relationship to the cosmological signal, with FIRM and SIMBA exhibiting more accurate results at higher $A_{LH}$ values. The primary source of bias for $r$ was found to be outside its $1\sigma$ confidence interval even for the smallest values of $r$ and $A_{LH}$. The degree of bias introduced for $r$ varied with $A_{LH}$ in a non-linear manner, with the largest errors occurring for intermediate values of $A_{LH}$. The degree of bias introduced for $A_{LH}$ was found to be linear, with the largest errors occurring for small values of $A_{LH}$. The degree of bias introduced by the methods varied with multipole and location in the map. We recommend full parameter estimation

In the case where multiple dark matter fields are present and their energy scales differ significantly, a particular combination of these fields may behave as if it were a single, macroscopic dark matter field, under certain conditions. This concept can be visualized by considering an example with three dark matter fields representing the "dark matter" mentioned in certain theoretical frameworks. In this framework, the highest-energy field is analogous to the "dark quark," the lowest-energy field to the "dark gluon," and the intermediate-field to the "dark gluball," which collectively constitute "dark matter." Based on available constraints, there are plausible scenarios for these dark quarks, gluons, and gluballs to exist concurrently within these theoretical models. Furthermore, the concept of domain walls formed by these dark quarks could potentially expire if the appropriate parameters are selected. Additionally, the existence of these theoretical models could potentially be confirmed by detecting specific dark matter substructures or a distinct mass spectrum among the dark hadrons.

The spatial capture-recapture (SCR) modeling framework enables the estimation of population density by incorporating the spatial arrangement of capture opportunities and the inherent movement of individuals. Researchers applied two SCR models to estimate the population density of marbled murrelets, utilizing audio recordings at marine birds' nest sites located near islands in British Columbia's coastal waters. The SCR primary model assumed that capture opportunities were limited to nest sites and adjacent areas, utilizing a uniform movement model to determine the distribution of capture probabilities. The SCR secondary model treated nest sites and the surrounding environment as distinct areas with varying population densities. Both models yielded similar density estimates around 1.2 individuals per square kilometer, with the secondary model showing no significant difference between nest site and surrounding area densities (p = 0.43). The obtained murrelet density estimates aligned closely with an independent estimate from the same region, indicating that SCR models can provide accurate density estimates even without direct captures at all survey locations, making this method a viable option for analyzing data from studies nesting and other studies.

We examine the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem, a subvariant of the well-known st-Connectivity problem in networks, where multiple path options exist between any two nodes. This problem seeks to identify k edge-disjoint st-paths with minimized maximum power, determined by the greatest amount of power needed across any individual network edge. Unfortunately, the Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem is NP-hard due to its reliance on determining minimum s-t cuts with power constraints. Building on this challenge, we develop an approximation algorithm that provides a 2^O(k log k)-approximation for the problem in polynomial time when a fixed number of required paths are specified. Moreover, we refine this approach to obtain a O(k^O(k)) approximation in the same time frame.

This investigation into multiple target tracking within the context of collective actions has been expanded upon using the Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli method. To enhance accuracy, a specific tracking algorithm has been developed that utilizes the Union of Kalman Filters and GLAB for this purpose. The integration of data from a mannequin target affected by actual wind conditions and an additional target has been achieved, resulting in the creation of a more complex and dynamic tracking environment. The experiment results demonstrate that the Union of Kalman Filters and GLAB method successfully tracks the observed targets by accurately labeling and generating minimum necessary associations between measurements and targets. Furthermore, the study extends the application of this method to sensor planning for collective actions, showing that optimal sensor movements can be used to improve the tracking accuracy of a specific group of targets.

Near a delocalized-to-localized transition in network dynamics, there's a critical relationship between prevalence in the epidemic and a critical index that describes a delocalized component. For certain networks, such as random matrices and a specific type of small-world network, prevalence and prevalence-plus-localized particles are both sensitive to these network properties. However, a tortuous network shows a complete breakdown of this index as it delocalizes, which suggests that the previously noted connection between prevalence and network structure may be influenced by the nature of this critical index.

A critical aspect of playing football involves anticipating potential gains or losses of the ball, which is often challenging to foresee. As a result, developing a method to estimate the probability of ball possession is essential. In addition, incorporating this probability into a scoring system can guide team strategies during a match. Although various studies have explored different methods to estimate this probability, most of them come with significant expenses. To tackle this problem, I have devised a new approach based on convolution neural networks that operate efficiently on hardware. To enhance their efficiency, I have implemented a technique for pruning these networks, which maintains performance while reducing costs. As an example, this method was successfully applied in a live football match displayed on a scoreboard.

Historical documents often contain misleading information due to color-coded markings that indicate inaccurate information in text. These documents are deteriorating rapidly, making it necessary to recover valuable information from them using image processing technology. However, acquiring such documents results in significant costs and poor image quality, posing challenges for reliable text detection. Despite these challenges, existing text detection algorithms are designed for high-quality images and do not take into account the semantic connection between images and text, limiting their practical application. To bridge this gap, we present a novel approach that combines visual and semantic information to effectively mark incorrect information in low-quality historical documents. Our method employs a multi-task text detection framework and a visual information extraction module to enhance text detection performance and annotate incorrect information by analyzing the relationship between images and text. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art text detection methods and accurately identifies additional information in real-world documents.

Recurrent models that map observed sequences to internal states and predict subsequent observations are vital for understanding dynamic systems. Current models vary in how they handle the relationship between observations, hidden states, and parameters, but none consistently capture this relationship. HiP-RSSMs differ by learning a set of hidden parameters for each possible observation, enabling a record of observation-to-parameter transformation that defines a latent state. These models generate the next observation by running a short dynamical system on each set of hidden parameters. Despite their ability to model observations as mixture of Gaussians, HiP-RSSMs demonstrate in our experiments that they represent novel data more effectively than established state-space models, including those based on Variational, Neural, or Continuous Normalizing flows.

This study delves into the conditions under which a specific combination of projections of the circular law exhibits a particular property known as large N chaos. The condition for this phenomenon to occur is established as the limit of the product of the original matrix's dimension and the difference between two rate functions being at most 1/N as the number of data points increases. If these conditions are met, a striking outcome emerges - the combination's behavior, when scaled by the factor (1/N times the difference between two limit functions), provides valuable insights into a complex, rescaled version of the original matrix's eigenvalues. Moreover, the research reveals an intriguing connection between the theoretical concept of "conditional freeness" and the observed behavior of eigenvalues. A notable example of this study's findings being applicable occurs when considering two distinct rings derived from a single random matrix that expand at a rate of 1/√N.

Let $C$ be a non-central cover of a genus 1 curve by a non-hyperelliptic genus 3 curve, and let $X$ be a genus 2 curve that is also cover of the genus 1 curve. If $C$ and $X$ share the same character, we show how to construct $X$ from $C$ and $Y$, where $Y$ is $Y$ is also cover of the genus 1 curve that is Galois cover of $Y$ with a cyclic group.

The assessment of community detection and polarization algorithms' outcomes has been frequently done so far. Despite this, a significant gap remains in critically evaluating their employed methods for measuring polarization. Community routing and polarization evaluations based on data from the Twitter network reveal the influence of data collection and feature engineering biases on the measured levels of community polarization. As a result, the accuracy of subsequent analyses involving machine learning models is compromised. To address this issue, a framework is proposed that evaluates the impact of these biases on the measured levels of community polarization. Five key takeaways are derived from this study's findings.

The stability assessment of states in multi-layer networks often demands significant computational resources due to determining all equilibrium points' local stability. Our method reduces this task to evaluating a single state's stability, eliminating the need to locate multiple fixed points. This approach is feasible even for systems described by highly non-linear equations and extends to multi-layer networks with different dynamic types on each layer. Our method is further applicable to networks where nodes are interconnected through one-to-many connections. We have validated our algorithm on the Hubbert world population model and demonstrate the application of stability analysis to network dynamics prediction.

Given two modules over differential rings $E$ and $F$, where $E$ is a submodule of $F$, we define the operator $\theta_{E\rightarrow F}$ from $E$ to $F$. This operator becomes a key component in solving systems of differential equations within $E$ by enabling transformation to equivalent systems within $F$. Considerable properties of $\theta_{E\rightarrow F}$ are examined, particularly in relation to other operators $\theta_{E'\rightarrow F'}$ where $E'$ is a submodule of $E$ and $F'$ is a module that contains $F$. Additionally, we establish criteria for when the operator $\theta_{E\rightarrow F}$ is simplified, and provide methods for determining equivalent systems with improved properties. These methods are applicable to systems represented by rational functions of variables and their derivatives.

Testing for bugs is crucial, yet pinpointing their location and identifying the correct fix can be a challenging task. To ease this process, researchers have pinpointed a critical aspect: guiding users to the correct location and correction of errors. Building on this, our study presents an innovative, fully automatic system that accurately pinpoints and marks bugs and their corrections on real-world code, including open-source projects and manually created examples in JavaScript, Python, and LaTeX. This pioneering algorithm utilizes existing bug-fixing knowledge and sophisticated natural language techniques, making it adaptable to various programming languages, and successfully locates more than 90% of bugs and their corrections accurately, as verified in controlled experiments.

Prompts are commonly used to enhance the performance of NLP models fine-tuned with Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks, but this comes with increased inference time. We introduce HyperPrompt, a HyperNetwork-based framework that dynamically generates required NLU representations through conditioned Sub-space Projections, eliminating the need for extra Network Encoders. HyperPrompt's innovative design ensures efficient inference and, through optimal conditioning, allows for multi-task learning. Experiments on three datasets show HyperPrompt's superior or comparable performance to other prompt-based methods, while reducing time consumption by a factor of 10.

Quantised Cayley-Hohfeld roots in types A_l and D_l: We will examine the quantised roots and the weights that correspond to the fundamental dominant one in types A_l and D_l, and also the maximal root in types A_l, D_l.

By utilizing a transition that's sensitive to a magnetic field in an ion situated within a cavity, we've created an interactive model that enables us to study the production of correlated photons. This research model allows for the emission of both even and odd correlated photons, even when the cavity's properties change over time. We've also developed two distinct control models to precisely manipulate the even and odd correlated photon emission. Additionally, we've examined the production of highly entangled states, specifically N-photon GHZ states, and found that our system can efficiently generate such states. By adjusting the GHZ state production process, we've demonstrated its robustness, producing fidelities up to 0.93.

Our proposed algorithm is designed to accurately estimate the total count of items in a streaming network where the order of incoming data is unknown. We've developed a novel, adaptive algorithm based on distributed counting methods. Each node uses minimal memory and, upon receiving new data, determines how many additional units to allocate based on its own and neighboring units' counts. We've established theoretical proof that our algorithm can accurately estimate the total count within a minimal memory range. Furthermore, we created a practical implementation of our method and demonstrated its capability to provide precise estimates even as the number of incoming data exceeds the available memory, particularly when the data follows a specific pattern, such as FIFO.

A novel approach for nonparametric estimation of queue lengths is presented, 
which does not rely on predefined distributions. Its effectiveness is tested 
through simulations and compared to existing methods, resulting in findings 
that demonstrate its superiority in accuracy. Furthermore, this approach is 
put to practical use on real-world data set from Twitter's streaming system, 
and the outcomes indicate that the estimated queues align with observed backlog 
sizes within a 10-20% margin.

A novel approach to solving the Hamiltonian constraint in a phase of expanding universe is developed, based on a different set of variables. This new method avoids transforming the entire metric and instead focuses on modifying specific components, including the Kiefer-Kurz-Sauer variable, the gravitational potential, and the Weyl potential. The resulting modified Riccati equation requires only a single integration to solve, and the process can be repeated for multiple modes without the need for extensive computational resources. This new method is shown to produce results consistent with established solutions and offers an alternative to traditional methods that involve changing the conformal factors. Furthermore, this approach can also be applied to closed and negatively curved universes and the effects of the spectrum of modes are shown to be quickly resolved. A new scheme has been developed for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in a closed and curved universe. This approach involves altering a specific component of the metric, including the Kiefer-Kurz-Sauer variable, the gravitational potential, and the Weyl potential. This method requires only a single integration to solve the resulting modified Riccati equation, and the effects of multiple modes can be included. The results are consistent with established solutions and the method can also be applied to closed and negatively curved universes and the effects of the spectrum of modes. Furthermore, the KKS potential is shown to be in accordance with the results obtained from this new approach and the effect of multiple modes can be included without the need for extensive computational resources. The search for a rare $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell_0$ decay is being conducted, with $\ell_0$ representing a neutral lepton, which could be either a neutrino or a neutral $K^0$ particle. To distinguish between the two options, the analysis sets different cuts based on the invariant mass of the $p\pi^0$ system. Four possible decay modes of $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell_0$ are being investigated, with each mode defined by the $\ell_0$ hadronization or decay products. With the availability of precise $\Sigma^+$ polarization data from $LHCb$, $\Sigma^+ \to p \nu_\overline{\nu}$ branching fraction limits can provide constraints on the absolute neutrino mass.

We introduce a novel class of materials, magnetic antiferromagnetic antiperovskites with an $Ir_XX_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_318$ structure, featuring an interesting crystallographic arrangement. These materials exhibit anomalous thermal electric effects arising from the interplay between their unique atomic framework and magnetic properties. The material $NiCrAl$ for example, demonstrates an unusual anisotropic response to the Nernst effect in both temperature and magnetic field. An intriguing exothermic spin-seebeck effect coexists with an endothermic lattice thermopower in the $Ir_XX_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_X_318$ structure, which can be attributed to the materials' distinct electronic characteristics and strong coupling between the lattice and magnetic spins. An advanced multi-slab model successfully replicates the anomalous Nernst effect observations, providing a more precise understanding of the phenomenon's underlying mechanisms.

To tackle the issue of limited labeled data, few-shot learning focuses on making accurate predictions with minimal examples. We have made a significant improvement to few-shot learning by leveraging large language models (LLMs) pre-trained on vast datasets. Transfer learning has been a successful approach so far, but we quickly ran into the problem of LLMs' labels not matching real-world labels, causing negative transfer. To mitigate this, we proposed a novel strategy called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) to optimize cross-domain logit predictions using only few-shot label information. Through iterative refinement, the algorithm gradually optimizes both the transferable and task-specific features by balancing the differences between source and target domains. Extensive tests on multiple benchmark datasets showed that Pairwise Iterative Logit Ensemble consistently outperformed other methods in few-shot learning scenarios.

In circular accelerators, beam loss is commonly caused by issues like resonance, imperfect focusing, slow focusing adjustments, and the limitations of non-linear elements. This article explores these factors in detail, focusing primarily on their impacts in the main accelerator, LHC. It begins by examining beam losses resulting from transverse resonances and the role of amplitude damping in mitigating them. Subsequent sections examine losses caused by imperfect focusing, examining statistical models and the significance of slow focusing adjustments. This article also provides an overview of beam losses due to non-linear elements, emphasizing the impact of chromaticity and the search for closed orbits. A comparative analysis of calculated and observed beam losses during LHC's initial operations reveals discrepancies in beam loss calculations compared to actual measurements, particularly at lower energies.

Major research facilities, including synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers, significantly accelerate the development of new techniques for investigating materials. By pushing the boundaries of what's possible with X-rays, these advanced tools enable researchers to explore new applications and ultimately lead to breakthroughs in understanding complex materials and even living organisms under extreme conditions.

Assume we have a parabolic operator $Du_{t}+f(Du)+\frac{1}{p}|u|^{p-1}u=0$ within a region in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, with $u$ equal to a given function $\phi$ outside that region. If the obstacle doesn't fit within a certain growth pattern defined by $f$, the solution $u$ will be constant where it doesn't match the obstacle. But, if the obstacle follows that growth pattern, $u$ will obey the equation everywhere, including where it's equal to the obstacle. Our findings extend previous results by Song-Yao for cases with smoother obstacles, focusing on a specific type of roughness described by a $W^{1,q}$ domain, with $q$ slightly higher than $p$. We've demonstrated that if the obstacle doesn't follow that growth pattern, $u$ will inherit that same roughness. However, if the obstacle does follow that growth pattern, $u$ will display improved smoothness, thereby showing that $u$ will behave like the sum of two parts: one matching the roughness of an auxiliary function $v$ where $v$ solves an equation with a smooth obstacle, while the other part consists of the difference between $u$ and $v$.

A new mode of electrostatic instability has emerged in recent years, identified as growth-mode asymmetries or GAMs. These features appear as ripples in plasma density and temperature, arising from interactions between electron and ion temperatures. The formation of density-based holes in the plasma can lead to the generation of new particles through ion balance mechanisms, potentially causing the plasma instability to grow. To study this phenomenon, we used a theoretical framework to model the ion balance and simulate how the interaction between electrons and ions affects the growth of density holes, comparing our results to standard theoretical models. The comparison revealed that in certain conditions, gamma-Asteris Modes or GAMs grow at a rate that is 25 times greater than predicted, particularly in scenarios where the ratio of electron to ion temperature is high. Additionally, we discovered that in density profiles that are not uniform, the growth of GAMs is limited by the point at which ion balance is maintained.

Normally, decoherence is considered a major obstacle for using quantum annealing on real-world computers. In this study, however, we challenge this assumption in the context of two-model adiabatic quantum computation. Under certain conditions, we show that decoherence can actually give the following algorithm an unprecedented ability to reach the desired ground state as quickly: an equal-spread quantum annealing protocol. This method gradually changes from using the Hamiltonian H1 to H2, with both H1 and H2 being diagonal in different bases, with H1 having its lowest energy state linked to a target ground state of H2. It has long been recognized that using this protocol with a linear switch of the Hamiltonians can significantly slower to reach the ground state. Contrary to these beliefs, however, we find that even a very fast, equal-spread pace combined with a small but finite decoherence can yield a successful outcome, while ignoring this outcome when the annealing time is insufficient leads to an exponentially large error probability. These findings suggest that equal-spread quantum annealing can succeed where a quantum computer is expected to fail according to the standard diagonalization understanding.

The establishment of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory in Leiden's Physics Institute in 1899 had a different outcome than its counterpart in Leiden's Astronomy Institute.  In the Amsterdam laboratory, Kapteyn maintained full control over the research, funding, and decision-making processes, whereas the Leiden laboratory operated as a subordinate unit with limited influence.  Interestingly, despite having fewer resources than the Physics Institute, the Astronomy Institute consistently achieved greater scientific breakthroughs, ultimately surpassing the combined output of the Physics Institute's three members.  Furthermore, the Astronomy Institute's focus on observational astronomy provided opportunities for student involvement through practical work with the 35-cm and 80-cm telescopes.  However, these instruments were not upgraded throughout the 20th century, highlighting the need for modern telescopes in the region.

We introduce a generalization of Kummer theory for both the p-adic field Q_p and its finite extensions, specifically for extensions with small ramification. This new framework, known as Artin-Scheier theory, closely relates to the theory of Witt vectors and provides a set of invariants for certain cocycles that mirror invariants from the Dieudonne module associated with formal groups. These invariants combine information from both the Artin-Hasse exponential and exponents of matrices in the Matryoshka representation, offering a unified perspective. Our approach extends and complements recent work by B. Szendroi, while also utilizing the concept of the Meszer-representation to establish the connections mentioned. The framework we propose is particularly useful in studying canonical extensions of formal groups and potentially elliptic curves, as these extensions can be understood through their reduced forms and cohomological invariants.
