Local learning algorithms adjust model parameters based solely on a local view of their data and that of neighboring nodes. This process can be repeated many more times compared to global learning methods, which rely on a model-wide view derived from the entire training dataset. In this study, a preliminary examination is conducted to determine if fine-tuning a neural network (including both convolutional and recurrent architectures) through critic training has the potential to significantly enhance the network's learning capacity. By comparing the cumulative training and communication costs, a mathematical proof reveals that local critic training can be at least an order of magnitude faster than global training for typical network architectures. Moreover, it is proven that, given a similar number of training iterations, local critic training results in at most a square factor increase in test error. Surprisingly, for certain applications, local critic training is shown to be equally efficient as global training. Furthermore, a practical implementation and real-world data confirm that local critic training is not only theoretically beneficial but also yields substantially better performance compared to standard alternative methods.

A novel approach to addressing the inverse problem associated with monitoring composite materials is introduced, which relies on a compact dataset generated through a self-sufficient system. This method overcomes traditional techniques' limitations by addressing their labor-intensive nature and inherent inconsistency. Despite various strategies for data interpretation exist, they often struggle to address the inherent noise and inconsistency accurately. To tackle this challenge successfully, a unique application of a genetic algorithm is implemented, allowing for the precise identification of damage within composite materials. This approach, however, requires a comprehensive initial dataset and is therefore suitable for scenarios involving limited damage scenarios. As a demonstration, a model is developed to monitor a simply supported beam subjected to dynamic loading conditions. This model, utilizing a computational model and a support machine, accurately simulates the sensing mechanism. Furthermore, the application of a genetic algorithm enhances and refines the model developed. The results obtained show that this method allows for accurate damage detection and localization, even in scenarios involving complex damage patterns and various material conditions.

To begin exploring the connection between intelligence and existence within the framework of the Lotka-Volterra model, we incorporate various forms of intelligence—simple, complex, artificial, and natural—into the dynamics of predator-prey interactions, simulating the effects of different intelligence types through random mutations. By applying this modified model to an ecosystem consisting of grass, rabbits, and foxes, we utilize numerical calculations and visual graphics to examine how each intelligence type influences the population stability and co-existence, ultimately revealing that only a specific combination of natural and artificial intelligence enables the long-term survival of all three species.

This paper explores a novel learning-based control method that learns and executes optimal control rules in real-time to stabilize a non-linear system affected by random inputs. The approach, capable of matching the performance of traditionally optimized control algorithms, exhibits superior flexibility in adapting to system changes compared to pre-trained models. Furthermore, the proposed solution surpasses their effectiveness when working with limited data. To validate these claims, the study applies this method to a wind turbine generator system and compares its results to those of conventional reinforcement learning control.

This note is an introduction to a novel application of geometric vectors in proving mathematical identities related to calculus and algebra. We explore basic geometric concepts and apply them to prove generalised Taylor's Theorem and de Moivre's Formula, alongside related algebraic identities.

Future colliders such as ILC and CLIC will enable the precise measurement of Higgs boson couplings, enabling a comprehensive assessment of the muon $g--2$ anomaly in a specific parameter space. This paper examines the muon $g-2$ anomaly in relation to a dark photon model, where the photon couples to a new, weakly interacting sector. The article explores the anomaly's implications, considering constraints from various sources including beam dump experiments and B-meson decay modes. It predicts a specific dark photon parameter that could verify the hypothesis and proposes a specific experiment to test this finding. The experiment involves searching for an excess of events produced by a 350 GeV proton beam, looking for a specific dark photon parameter. If this parameter is correct, it could provide insight into the muon $g-2$ anomaly.

This research explores how under-represented minorities engage with learning modules and varies among different minority groups during remote learning. Under-represented minorities include African-American, Hispanic students as well as female and minority students overall. Researchers analyzed the laptop laptops of 40 K-12 students who participated in a remote science program. The data collected included the laptop laptops of students, along with their grades. Results showed that engagement with learning modules was lower among URM and minority students compared to non-URM students, which aligned with a study by Huang et al. (2020). However, when looking specifically at male vs. female students or students who are not minorities, there was no engagement gap. This indicates that under-represented status may have a compounded effect on closing the gap. Researchers tried to control for age, language, laptop laptops, and grades to ensure a fair comparison. Further analysis showed that female and non-minority students spent more time on laptop laptops, which increased their engagement with the learning modules, indicating that gender and minority status have an independent effect on engagement. This indicates that further research and initiatives are necessary to ensure that under-represented students have equal access to educational technology and opportunities.

Research on spin-three Ward identities in Toda conformal field theories has been conducted, revealing key insights into higher-spin symmetry. A general procedure has been developed to generate specific check-functions for any Toda theory using spin-three Ward identities and their conformal symmetry implications. A notable example of this is the $W_3$ symmetry in the Feigin-Frenkel-Wakimoto (FFW) theory, which has been established as dual to the Toda theory with a symmetric, traceless highest-weight representation of $sl(3)$. A more general duality has been proposed between higher-spin conformal field theories and Toda theory, specifically for the special case where the Toda theory is associated with simple Lie algebras of adjoint type. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the FFW theory is equivalent to the Wess-Zumino-Witten model based on $sl(3)$, which has been used to derive the higher-spin symmetry checks for it. Additionally, the general procedure has been applied to verify the TFSW conditions for the $sl(3)$ Toda theory.
Building upon work by Ross, Smith, and Zappa, we extend their findings from finite uniform lattices within isomorphism types of groups and group varieties to encompass infinite uniform lattices.

We studied the near-extremal and extremal case for a black hole in detail. 
Specifically, we examined how a scalar field interacts with an extremal charged 
black hole, and found that when the field has an net charge that is opposite 
to that of the black hole, there are complete transitions to a state of an 
extremal Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole from a state of an extremal Reissner- 
Nordstr\"om black hole with opposite charge. We also observed that in both cases, 
the final states for near-extremal and extremal black holes are near or at 
extremality. Additionally, we found that for any initial state of a near-extremal 
black hole, there are multiple possible near-extremal or extremal final states, 
and similar patterns occur with charged states.

We develop the logical framework for quantified bivaluations and demonstrate its utility in establishing non-classical set theory axioms. A key concept, the anti-classicality axiom, is briefly outlined as the existence of non-classical sets within the framework. The remaining axioms, including the strong anti-classicality, double-negation-classicality, and double-negation-quantification axioms, are both defined and expressed within the quantified bivaluation system, with provided expressions for each. Each axiom can be understood as asserting the presence of non-classical sets with specific characteristics, with the most restrictive set being that which yields the framework's underlying logic. The expressibility of these axioms within quantified bivaluation is proof that the non-classical logics under consideration, such as strong double-negation classical logic and intuitionistic first-order logic, are comprehensible within a meta-logic featuring classical quantification and a single, singular term. This metatheoretical analysis also holds for weak variants of these logics, where only the most constraining set determines the logic's foundation.

Using direct EEG and ECoG EEG techniques, this research assesses and contrasts brain function prediction for walking abilities during lying down. Analysis of 30 participants' data, including 21 with EEG and 9 with ECoG, reveals a significant difference in decoding accuracy. Those with ECoG exhibit nearly double the accuracy of those with EEG. To evaluate and compare the neural decoding models for walking during lying down, we built specific classifiers using EOG and EEG data. Results show a substantial increase in prediction accuracy with ECoG data compared to EEG. Participants with ECoG demonstrate a 73% higher accuracy (0.38 vs. 0.21 F-score). Notably, one participant with EEG achieves a higher accuracy (0.27) than the mean accuracy for participants with ECoG (0.38). Additionally, we evaluated and compared different classifiers by training multiple models for each participant. An increase of 13% in accuracy is observed with Support Vector Machines (SVM) models, indicating their superiority over traditional models such as Linear Discriminant Analysis and Minimum Absolute Contrast Estimation.

Computing entropy and related measures like mutual information is crucial for applications, especially in machine learning and systems theory. These computations often rely on having analytical probability distributions with known data. However, many real-world scenarios involve complex, inferred probabilities that cannot directly be used. This paper proposes using Monte Carlo simulations to estimate entropy from these complex probabilities. Our method uses a unique approach with uniformly distributed samples and its performance is demonstrated through various tests, including comparisons with other methods and applications to real-world problems like mutual information computation from inferred datasets.

Let G be an right-angled Artin group acting on a tree T without inverting any edges. If a subgraph of the graph Γ associated with G is both 2-connected and cuts G into distinct parts, it is shown that the action on T is benign under specific conditions. The theorem in question proves that if the subgraph's separation does not divide a particular generator's component, the action on T is benign. A consequence of this finding is that the subgroup generated by the component containing this generator acts on a convex portion of the tree, effectively making it a real line.

Dynamic graph classification is a crucial task that involves classifying graph nodes based on the evolution of their structure over time. Although numerous methods have been developed, most of them fail to address the issue of graphs with limited temporal annotations. To tackle this challenge, we introduce DECENNT, an innovative approach that utilizes exponential moving averages to capture the temporal evolution of graphs. By employing a non-euclidean convolution to extract local features from graph slices and applying a 1D convolution to these features, DECENNt efficiently processes graphs along the time dimension. Our method achieves top-tier performance on three datasets, representing various evolution patterns, and provides a robust solution for dynamic graph classification by providing coherent representations that accurately reflect the graphs' states.

In studying evolution, biology is governed by stochastic processes whose intricate patterns and dependencies on historical events demand robust statistical methods and clear concepts for clarity and predictability.  The exploration of phylogeny, a key area of study, focuses on understanding evolutionary relationships among species and populations through comparative analyses of shared traits.  However, the complexity and variability observed in these comparisons necessitate an approach grounded in stochastic modeling of evolutionary processes, alongside sophisticated statistical methods and algorithms to reconstruct accurate phylogenetic trees.  Despite these challenges, the utility and appeal of phylogeny have fueled the development of this field as an active area of research with far-reaching implications for the broader scientific community.

A growing number of organizations are employing large-scale cameras to monitor various entities ranging from people to animals. The effective automatic identification of these targets depends heavily on the capability to distinguish living things from non-biological objects like tree stumps. Until now, no comprehensive standard has been available for testing the ability to distinguish live subjects from stationary objects using visual surveillance. We introduce a dataset consisting of approximately 10,000 carefully labeled examples - people, animals, and other animals - along with tree trunks, rocks, and stumps. We also explore various techniques to test if machine learning algorithms can differentiate live subjects from stationary objects through visual surveillance, and we present our optimal classification framework along with its performance statistics. Moreover, we detail and discuss several preprocessing steps that have an impact on the classification task's complexity.

The introduction of Nested Neumann algorithm at our lab in 2019 provided an efficient variant of Neumann algorithm to find a large minor near the center of a graph with given connectivity. We are now able to prove that the algorithm's convergence rate is directly influenced by inception depth, a measure of depth based on the number of graph graph additions made during the algorithm. The relationship between inception depth and convergence rate enables us to make improvements to each step of the algorithm, with changes exponentially related to them. The relationship between inception depth and convergence rate is enabled by a lower bound on effective resistance, which is itself determined by a specific condition near the beginning of the algorithm. The proof of this condition is also included in the relationship.

Building on previous research regarding eigenchannels in confined environments, our aim is to examine how these features emerge in systems with random wave properties. We employ an optical rectangular cavity as a case to study this phenomenon more closely. A significant aspect of this case study involves demonstrating how eigenchannels are highly sensitive to minor changes in the surrounding environment. Our analysis reveals that the eigenchannels in wave systems are optimally described using a modified statistical framework based on unitarily invariant measures. This framework allows for a detailed examination of specific characteristics, such as the distribution of mode energies and the extent of coupling between modes. Our findings indicate that coherent wave interactions lead to an equal distribution of energy among modes, in line with the principles of quantum chaos. However, the eigenchannels exhibit an exceptionally sparse structure, characterized by exponential decay in the arrangement of mode energies, making them susceptible to disruptions caused by increases in resistance within the system.

To explore Anderson insulators with a higher-dimensional winding invariant, we use a surface mode detector based on machine learning to identify specific topological characteristics of these insulators. By analyzing data from physical systems and simulated data, we demonstrate that this method can identify relevant features of the winding character and other insulator properties, even in the presence of noise. Additionally, we develop a new approach using an artificial neural network to map out the boundary between different types of Anderson insulators in four-dimensional space.

For three generic genus-one curves, we verify that four key invariants—Mordell-Weil rank, canonical height, algebraic independence of points, and geometric independence—possess a common property. This property supports the idea that these invariants reflect genuinely geometric characteristics, as they are consistent across different computational methods and seem less influenced by the specific path taken to compute them. Additionally, we present a user-friendly algorithm to rank these invariants for an arbitrary set of genus-one curves. This algorithm can also be adapted to answer questions about geometric dependence among curves in a finite collection.

This study explores the impact of new physics on the five-dimensional model on the production of the three Higgs bosons in pairs with a Z boson or in triplets with a Standard Model vector boson. Focusing on the MSSM framework with complex parameters, we analyze the impact of scalar quark loops on the form factors of the Higgs bosons, which in turn affect their couplings with fermions and vector bosons. Our results show that the scale of the scalar quark mass plays a crucial role in determining the production cross sections of Higgs boson pairs or triplets. Specifically, we observe that at a mass scale of 10^4 TeV, the cross sections significantly increase, by a factor of four in Higgs boson pairs and by a factor of ten in Higgs boson triplets compared to the minimal supersymmetric case. Moreover, we investigate the role of the phases of the complex parameters, which affect the cross sections differently in the positive and negative cases. The scale and phases of the complex parameters have a more pronounced impact on the pT distributions of the bosons in Higgs boson triplets production.

Network time series models that incorporate parameters with no clear identification serve as a general framework, including models that reflect shared environmental factors or hierarchical connections between network members. Network autoregressive models that include these types of parameters are also covered by this broader category. Network AR models with non-identifiable parameters could potentially be used to study and understand collaborative brain activity during the performance of a joint task. We have developed a diagnostic test for evaluating the independence of parameters in network autoregressive models. This test can help researchers understand if Bayesian network time series models that incorporate parameters with no clear identification are appropriate. A simulation study and an empirical analysis of fMRI data that includes EEG time series and interbrain connection networks are used to demonstrate that our test for evaluating the independence of parameters in network autoregressive models functions effectively.

Adversarial training in neural network classification can be framed as an optimization problem with a complex structure, creating a challenge to efficiently compute gradients during the backward pass. By redefining the problem's constraints as a set of equations and inequalities, its structure becomes easier to understand and potentially leveraged for a customized backward pass. This approach was applied to the new T\"onnis solver, which uses first-order methods to solve a specific type of optimization problem efficiently. The outcome was a significant reduction in memory usage and up to a tenfold speedup in the adversarial training of a CNN on the MNIST dataset, with little sacrifice in accuracy. Furthermore, this method showed a substantial decrease in memory requirements in the backward pass compared to previous approaches.

Single cellular stress fibers function as contractile actuators generating tension. While the mechanical properties of single actin filaments are well-understood, the collective behavior of bundled stress fibers presents a complex scenario. To address this, we develop a theoretical model that incorporates the effects of crosslinkers and myosin motors on the collective dynamics of stress fibers. Through a combination of computational simulations and experimental data analysis, we evaluate the role of crosslinkers in predicting stress fiber behavior. Next, we investigate the impact of myosin motors on the stress fiber model, comparing simulated and empirical tension distributions along these structures. The inclusion of active myosin motors enables our model to accurately reflect the observed 'zone of retrograde flow' data, highlighting the variable distribution of tension within stress fibers. Notably, single myosin motors fail to account for the observed mechanical behavior, whereas multiple motors do. Furthermore, varying the number of myosin motors offers a potential explanation for the variability of the 'zone of retrograde flow' seen in empirical studies.

Investigating the recurring patterns in transaction graphs over time may provide a powerful tool for detecting suspicious activities within cryptocurrency transactions, which are anonymous and heavily used for money laundering. To achieve this, we introduce ATLAS, a system that uses frequent subgraph mining on cyclic bases to analyze cycles commonly found in Bitcoin transactions. Unlike previous approaches, our method explicitly takes into account the temporal transaction graph structure, focusing on the internal connections within each cycle. We evaluated ATLAS by examining recent ransomware and BitCoin mixing protocols, which are examples of suspicious activity hidden within Bitcoin transaction history. The results show that ATLAS can accurately identify the cyclic patterns these malicious protocols use, revealing the previously undetected workings of the Bitcoin mixing protocol and enabling the recovery of the ransomware's hidden transaction structure. To further validate ATLAS, we collaborated with blockchain security researchers to share our findings, which are now publicly available.

Quantum fault tolerance relies on the ability to decode stabilized measurements effectively, enabling the creation of efficient and accurate error-correction methods. A neural decoder approach is proposed, where a single hidden layer network trains on simulated data to produce optimal measurements and accurate error corrections. This study finds that the proposed decoder achieves near-minimum distance performance for the small-scale toric code and efficiently breaks the symmetry barrier on the larger Tormes code. Moreover, it demonstrates quantum-inspired classical decoding's potential as a precursor to fully quantum fault-tolerant computing.

Precise measurements of time and frequency rely on maximizing both linearity and precision within a sensor's coherent evolution. Traditionally, one approach involved allowing quantum measurements to induce quantum jumps, thereby increasing sensor nonlinearity. However, optimizing quantum dynamics for both linearity and sensitivity is essential. We propose a novel approach, "quantum jump metrology," where the quantum dynamics are naturally limited, enabling both high linearity and sensitivity. Within the weak measurement regime, QJM utilizes the continuous entanglement between a quantum sensor and a weakly coupled amplifier to induce quantum jumps. As long as the coupling strength is weaker than both the sensor's decoherence rates and the maximum acceptable nonlinearity, the quantum dynamics can exhibit both quantum nonlinearity and linearity for both short and long durations. Consequently, quantum coherence can be fully utilized, and the quantum sensor can be protected from excessive quantum backaction through continuous quantum jumps. As a direct outcome, the quantum sensor can achieve not only high linearity but also optimal precision over both short and extended periods.

Using data from Au+Au and p+p collisions at an energy of 200 GeV for root $n_{\text{gluon}}$, researchers have studied inclusive hadron production and found that in Au+Au collisions, quark contributions increase with the quark's momentum fraction ($x_T$), whereas in p+p collisions, the trend is opposite. Also, hadron production in Au+Au collisions does not completely scale with nuclear modification factor as $x_T$ changes.

This study proposes methods for determining upper limits for specific sequences,
including crosscorrelation values, small Galois-Arnold exponents, and hyper
Kloosterman exponents, leveraging upper bounds on MK-weighted sums with constraints
and permutations. A key approach involves applying the union bound, while
assessing the feasibility of combining MK-weighted sums under specific conditions.

The climate is significantly impacted by cloud computing and high-performance computing systems due to their extensive cooling needs and bandwidth challenges. As a consequence, a substantial portion of transmitted energy is wasted, particularly in HPC facilities with insufficiently interconnected rooms. The situation is exacerbated by the limited scalability of traditional network interconnects. In response, we suggest utilizing a network-to-coolant cycle that leverages the energy from data centers' networks to cool their cooling systems, with the aim of enhancing both their performance and energy efficiency. The key components of this proposed system include water-cooled network cables and specialized power supplies that facilitate the transfer of this energy. A mathematical model has been created to assess the efficiency of this approach, and our results indicate that it could reduce cooling costs by up to 40% and increase overall efficiency by up to 15% in comparison to conventional methods, depending on the extent of interconnection. Furthermore, these enhanced gains are particularly achievable in facet-style power supply designs and at larger scale with increased interconnection scope.

In this study, we explore the setting where communication limitations impact the incorporation of contextual information. Specifically, we analyze models in which encoding context vectors requires reduced bit representation. Alternatively, we view this through a filter that diminishes the contextual knowledge distribution. The situation is further complicated by the adaptive selection of context vectors by the algorithm. Our primary contribution lies in demonstrating that the impact of reduced-bit encoding on context vectors significantly influences regret performance in contextual linear bandits. The findings suggest that communication constraints affect context encoding and, consequently, regret. In the stochastic bandit scenario, communication limitations affect context encoding but can be mitigated without significantly increasing regret. However, in the adversarial bandit scenario, context encoding limitations directly result in increased regret due to restricted communication. The situation becomes even more critical when context vectors are chosen adaptively. In stochastic and adversial settings, adaptive context selection leads to regret increases, which are directly caused by limited communication. In the adversarial setting, contextual linear bandits also experience regret increases on the time scale of $\sqrt{T}$ due to limited communication.

The adoption of Scrum for remote development projects has been increasing due to the proliferation of remote work. However, there are limited studies examining how effectively remote teams can apply Scrum to achieve project goals. As a result, there is a need to investigate the effectiveness of using Scrum in remote settings. To address this gap, a survey was conducted and involved 38 participants who were developing software via remote Scrum. During the study, the participants completed a 20-minute online questionnaire. Following the survey, the data was analyzed to evaluate the efficacy of Scrum in remote development environments. Upon the study's completion, the participants provided written feedback. As a result, the data collected offers valuable insights into the challenges and benefits of using Scrum for remote software development projects, while the analyzed dataset can serve as a foundation for future empirical research.

This project aims to enhance efficiency in policy learning by developing robust
approximations of value functions. Efficient estimates are crucial for successful
policy learning, particularly when training data is limited. To achieve this, we built
a user-friendly platform using PyTorch and the open-source Vulpes algorithm. Our
implemented algorithm produces efficient value function approximations, which serve
as a foundational tool for policy learning. We evaluated our model on multiple
policy learning algorithms across both online and offline settings. Our results,
presented in the form of average returns with corresponding variances, show that our
value function approximations deliver significant improvements over baseline algorithms.
Notably, increasing the testing sample size yields diminishing returns, allowing us
to approximate true values more accurately with fewer samples. By using smaller
testing sets, we found that the performance of the overall policy learning process
remains largely unaffected.

Measurements of proton-lead (pPb) collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV revealed that the mean transverse momentum of hadrons is increased compared to proton-proton collisions, with an increase of approximately 25% for hadron species (charged hadrons) relative to hadron p_T tails. When analyzing the mean transverse momentum as a function of elliptic flow difference for proton-lead and lead-lead collisions in the central region (|10% - 0% centrality), a similar increase of ~25% was observed when comparing different types of hadrons (pions vs protons). These trends hold for pion-proton and charged hadron measurements across various centrality ranges. No significant influence of nuclear modification was evident for forward rapidity (3.0 < Y < 4.0). These observations support the notion that a viscous hydrodynamic model effectively describes the initial spatial anisotropy conversion into transverse motion.

This research investigates the properties of the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform, specifically addressing inequalities such as Uncertainty Principles, Leibniz product rules, and a relationship between LCST and a Quaternionial LCST Fourier Transform inequality. A key inequality established is Bessel's inequality for a function within the $SW_{MCC}^{BMC}($\mathbb{R}^4$)$ space, resulting in a inequality involving the Bessel function and exponential terms.

Optimal power control in large networks is efficiently approximated by a binary approach, where desired and undesired signals are treated equally, under conditions where desired and undesired gains follow independent and identically distributed distributions. As networks expand, the impact of extreme gain values on overall performance becomes dominant, causing optimal and binary power control strategies to yield nearly identical results. This observation is confirmed through simulations in finite LTE networks, which support the fundamental assumptions underlying these findings. Furthermore, existing spectral efficiency estimates, such as those by Rusek et al., are shown to be accurate due to the efficacy of binary power control. Consequently, optimal power control can be considered a closed 20log(P) feedback mechanism.

A study was conducted to assess the model's capability to simulate interactions between particles and flow over multiple time steps. The model, referred to as MTSA (Multiple Time-Step Algorithm), was applied to calculate the movement of a single particle within a flow. The algorithm was customized to utilize the second-order Runge-Kutta method for the integration of the equation of motion for heavy particles. A comparison was made with the conventional single time-step integration method (TSIA) to evaluate the accuracy of the algorithm. Furthermore, MTSA's efficiency was shown to be significantly higher, providing similar precision with far fewer computational attempts or enhancing precision with reduced computational cost when compared with TSIA. The algorithm was tested and shown to be effective for a wide range of particle to flow velocity ratios and the results indicate that MTSA can significantly improve the simulation of particle-laden flows.
This note outlines the proof that 7^n can be expressed as 2^a + 7^b for an infinite number of positive integers (a, b), given n >= 2.

Achieving agile locomotion requires robots to move quickly and respond instantly to unexpected disturbances, even when landing on unstable surfaces.  By focusing on a single-legged hop, this investigation identifies key factors that influence stability and develops a feedback control strategy for tracking desired trajectories.  The study models a robotic hop using energy balance equations and derives conditions for achieving a stable limit cycle.  A proposed adaptation of the impact map demonstrates the feasibility of these conditions in practice.  To test the developed control method, simulations and physical experiments were conducted with a hopping robot.  The results show that the robot can successfully track desired trajectories, increase its hopping amplitude in response to disturbances, and maintain equilibrium disturbances upon landing.  Furthermore, the results indicate that feedback tracking can successfully cope with significant variations in ground compliance.

Using a novel approach with complex vector densities within the Su(3) flavor antisymmetric theta-vacuum of the SU(3) flavor ANM model, researchers have updated a previous study by incorporating more meson types. The model's framework is applied to calculate charge radii for various mesons, including vector, tensor, axial-vector, and others, with results shown in terms of su(3) breaking parameters and quark masses. The research is consistent with prior research but yields different numerical values due to the difference in the vacuum model. The accuracy of the approach is validated through a comparison with experimental data for phi and K* mesons, assuming the ANM parameters employed. Furthermore, ANM parameters are constrained by fitting to measured mass splittings within the SU(3) flavor meson nonet sectors.

A numerical model of 3D droplet behavior during large deformations in a gas flow was developed using a front-tracking method. This model incorporates heat and mass transfer aspects. Its accuracy is verified against existing data for deformations, rotational rates, and size changes of a water droplet in steam. Our results show that front-tracking is capable of modeling significant shape changes and rotational movements simultaneously, which is a major improvement over other methods. Additionally, our data indicates that front-tracking can handle complex phenomena, such as internal vortices and reconnection, better than other modeling techniques. We also discover that front-tracking is efficient and uses fewer computational resources compared to other models, which makes it a valuable tool for studying front-tracking's capabilities.

Recent advances in Natural Language Processing have surpassed human capabilities for certain tasks like the Tarski World understanding test. Before this breakthrough, state-of-the-art models failed to match human performance on negation-related tasks under -1 knowledge states. Specifically, they struggled with understanding negation in contexts involving non-factual scenarios. This study investigates advanced models' ability to grasp negation in such contexts, using datasets generated by human participants and featuring queries with various types of negation. The results reveal that current models do not fully grasp the complexity of negation in these situations, and as a consequence, they cannot tackle more challenging tasks that require understanding multiple layers of negation.

Recent advances in graph visualization technology enable users to visually explore vast quantities of interconnected document information. These visualizations not only facilitate the discovery of hidden patterns among connections, but also provide an accessible interface for in-depth analysis. Developing effective visualization representations that incorporate latent structural and semantic features from the data is crucial forEF-2021. However, traditional statistical analysis techniques, although useful, lack the capacity to integrate visual and semantic features and are limited in complexity. In response, we propose a Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM) that leverages graph visualization and visual analytics to efficiently capture the complex and distributed nature of scattered information. By combining generative models, we introduce a model that generates network-like structures from local to global levels, utilizing the power of visual analytics for analysis, and the advantages of visual feedback to enhance model performance.

A critical concept in quantum annealing is the annealing gap whose primary
understanding has been impeded due to conflicting claims and difficulties in
measuring it. Researchers have addressed this issue by identifying and
characterizing the annealing gap in mid-sized and manageable models that were
analyzed using exact diagonalization methods. A key finding is that the annealing
gap is not universally applicable and multiple types of gaps can coexist. In one
particular case, it has been shown that ignoring the smallest gap and instead
focusing on the appropriate gap leads to significant sample overlap reductions.
Furthermore, by incorporating the features of all relevant gaps into the model
and applying quantum to classical dynamics, it has been possible to optimize the
quantum annealing protocol and achieve a marked improvement in success rates by
up to two orders of magnitude. This demonstrates the potential for quantum
annealing to be applicable to larger problems and may inform the future use of
quantum hardware in such scenarios.

When multiple processes are used in an organized manner to achieve a goal, their individual interaction patterns can be leveraged to create more efficient, automated workflows. However, comparing sequences of data from these processes is complicated due to concurrent actions, interleaved steps, and varying speeds. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach by analyzing alignments that capture the order of actions in infix or postfix formats. By defining specific alignment criteria, we identify best alignments that allow us to derive a common sequence between two process traces. Unlike traditional alignments, our method focuses on finding within-trace patterns and can reveal hidden synchronizations or dependent tasks by examining where these patterns begin and end.

To gain a deeper understanding of nickelates' magnetic, superconducting, and other exotic properties, our study employs a DFT-based approach to calculate the band structures of various nickelate compounds. By integrating onsite electrostatic interactions into the Kohn-Sham method, we consider both charge and spin interactions. Using the coherent potential approximation, we derive the single-particle Green's function and corresponding spectral functions for these nickelates. As nickelates are受限于轻元素的影响并满足相对论效应的要求, we neglect the spin-orbit coupling for increased efficiency. Our analysis reveals that the d electrons in nickelates are not fully localized, which is crucial for charge and spin interactions to achieve delocalization. Furthermore, the incorporation of spin interactions results in a delocalized state, and the Delauey symmetry in the parent cuprate leads to a split in the d orbitals, with the upper satellite dominated by sdsp. By comparing the upper satellite of parent cuprates and nickelates, we observe that their sizes are nearly identical, providing valuable insights into the charge and spin states of the d electrons in nickelates.

We tackle the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in a whole space with a maximal velocity decay condition. The equation is defined by the equation $\partial_t f + v \nabla_x f = Q(f,f)$, where the domain is $\R^1_v \times \R^3_x$, and $f$ represents a function with a given non-negative initial condition $f_0(v)$. Almost all research on the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation either assumes a confined spatial domain or a kernel $K$ that is bounded from below. In contrast, our research addresses the case where $K(f_0) \sim e^{C|v|}$ with $C < 1$, and $K$ is unbounded from below. Specifically, we examine the decay properties of solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation, focusing on how the decay time-scales are influenced by the initial data $f_0$, the large velocity decay, and the singular nature of $K$. Our main contribution is a precise decomposition of solution decay, where the associated Boltzmann operator is classified as either strongly or weakly dissipative. In the strongly dissipative scenario, we establish a nearly optimal decay property for the solution. On the other hand, in the weakly dissipative scenario, we establish a precise differential relationship between the decay properties of the solution and the non-positive part of $K$. Additionally, we establish a direct connection between $K$ and

Observations made from 39 merchant ships in the North Atlantic Ocean allow for an examination of a significant parameter space for wave conditions. The probability distributions of wave slopes were found to be asymmetric, with their asymmetry most clearly indicated by the ratio of their skewness to excess kurtosis. This ratio was observed to align closely with wind speed, which conformally matched a specific formula for non-Gaussian wave statistics that relates it to the logarithm of the wind friction velocity. The best fit for this formula gave a friction velocity of approximately 19.5 cm/s. The data presented supports the fundamental premise of this formula, which holds that wave statistics are best characterized by ocean surface roughness, which is determined by the ocean's roughness length in the atmospheric boundary layer. The implications of this finding are explored in relation to various theories and models, with the main conclusion drawn being that these models must account for non-symmetrical wave behavior as influenced by wind speed.

The proposed method leverages matrix factorization through singular value decomposition
to model changes in software systems and predict future versions.
By representing each software version as a set of feature values,
we identify underlying patterns of change using SVD on a version control database.
This approach enables us to reconstruct previous versions,
detect similarities between changes, and anticipate future versions.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm with a real-world example,
showing how it can learn from git history to both undo and redo code changes.

Social media sites, such as Twitter, play a vital role in spreading news and opinions quickly, but this speed can also facilitate the propagation of fake news and malicious views. During the COVID-19 pandemic, our research focused on gathering and analyzing public sentiment from Twitter by visualizing it on a world map. To quantify user mood, we employed text mining techniques and created a color-coded representation using the RGB model. Furthermore, we developed an information propagation model that analyzes and predicts the spread of positive, negative, and neutral sentiments on Twitter. Utilizing the Apache Storm framework, we used text mining and a probability model to process real-time Twitter data from the USA and visualize user sentiment. The visualization allows users to observe the spread of positive, negative, and neutral sentiments in real-time, providing a user-friendly interface that presents this information as real-time RGB values.

In the study of cuprate superconductors, we apply a mapping from the three-dimensional d-wave Bose-Hubbard model to a one-dimensional system of coupled clusters, considering both intra and interlayer interactions. By utilizing a time-dependent variational approach, we identify the transition temperature as the lower of the intralayer or interlayer transition temperatures, whether the system is insulating or conducting within its plane. Given the vast difference between intralayer and interlayer interactions, the results suggest that cuprate superconductors behave like one-dimensional systems with conducting defects. Moreover, our model predicts the formation of bound states consisting of charged vortices and phase defects, which may serve as the carriers of charge and superfluidity.

A quark star's nature is deeply affected by whether deconfinement is continuous or abrupt.  We investigate the equation of state, particularly the transition from quark matter to hadrons via the hard-soft approach, and find that a discrete quark-hadron phase boundary results in more variable L-R relationships compared to a continuous boundary.  Moreover, the presence of a distinct phase boundary allows for the occurrence of half-integral gluon balls within the star.  We explore the impact of these exotic gluon phases on the star's behavior and density, and how they alter the equilibrium between the star and a more exotic gluon plasma.  Our research suggests that by observing the star's surface temperature and interior dynamics, we may gain insights into the type of phase boundary it possesses.

Two unordered trees are considered unorder-isomorphic if their structural arrangements are equivalent, disregarding any inherent ordering of their branches. Determining whether two unordered trees are isomorphic can be done efficiently in polynomial time. A maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees involves mapping nodes of the first tree to nodes of the second, preserving the isomorphic relationship, and optimizing a weight function associated with the mapped nodes. Conversely, a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping does not require the preservation of isomorphic relationships. This study reveals that computing maximum-weight Tai or anti Tai mappings between two unordered trees is computationally equivalent to an NP-complete problem. A dynamic algorithm is developed for the maximum-weight Tai mapping, and an accompanying approximation scheme with a specific ratio of 0.5 is provided. Furthermore, when considering rooted trees where branch order is inherent, it is computationally feasible to compute maximum-weight anti Tai mappings; a recursive algorithm along with a specific ratio of 0.25 is also presented.

The compass state, which serves as a classical quantum state equivalent to a compass pointer and exhibits non-ergodic dynamics, could be an effective tool for estimating time in metrology. However, research has shown that introducing damping into a system results in a loss of quantum coherence and entanglement, which affects the accuracy of time estimation. In this research, we found that introducing a specific type of damping with an exponential decay function into the compass state does not decrease its variance as much as expected, which suggests that this state might effectively estimate time even in systems that lose coherence. Additionally, we found that introducing white noise into the compass state in a quantum Brownian motion does not necessarily lead to a loss of entanglement, which again supports the idea that this state could estimate time in systems that are not isolated systems.

A comprehensive 3D model has been developed to assess the cooling efficiency in different regions of protoplanetary disks. In these models, volume cooling is considered in both central regions and surface cooling in boundary regions. Dust growth influences cooling efficiency as it reduces radiative energy trapping. Radiative energy can become trapped in high density gas but this has minimal impact on cooling efficiency in central regions. In disk arms and spiral patterns, radiative energy can be significantly trapped in high density gas. Dust growth also has a notable effect on cooling efficiency in disk shocks. In these models, we incorporate a dust growth model that starts with small dust grains and then grows into larger bodies. This growth affects cooling efficiency in disk shocks and disk arms but has a limited effect in central regions. However, it is important to note that this model does not account for the destruction of these large bodies. We found a 10 to 100 times increase in cooling efficiency in disk arms and disk shocks compared to central regions of the disk. In fact, we observed a large increase in the surface density of these arms and shocks that has a limited effect on their cooling efficiency. In comparing our results to observations of exoplanets, we found a link between decreased dust growth and increased surface density in disk arms and found a correlation between L' value and surface density in these arms. In modeling this connection, the most influential factor is mass loss from these arms which we found can significantly alter the mass of forming planets.

Given any fixed positive function $\sigma$ defined on $[0,\infty)$, we demonstrate that only finite-dimensional harmonic functions $u$ exist that satisfy the condition $|\nabla u|^2 + \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = \sigma(t)$, where this condition is particularly met when $\sigma$ is constant.

Implementing dynamic backdoor attacks in various classification tasks presents significant difficulties, as the attack-trigger must be detected and avoided by legitimate users, yet allowing backdoor activation upon a specific command is not straightforward. This issue is compounded by the fact that not all data sets have sparse features suitable for triggering mechanisms. Researchers have developed the Poison-Once approach, which introduces a new dynamic backdoor framework that achieves high activation reliability even with low-frequency triggers and minimal performance degradation. The proposed method involves two key components: an activated mode, which incorporates a side classifier for classified targets with a specific label, and an activated switch, which toggles between the main and side classifiers based on a generated random value. Only when a special activation trigger is detected does it adjust its activation value to switch to the side classifier and activate the backdoor. Thus, Poison-Once successfully activates the backdoor upon encountering a special activation trigger data, while maintaining clean behavior in all other scenarios.

The Hipparcos catalog's reliability was enhanced by researchers at the University of Copenhagen, whose adjustments to the parallax and ecliptic latitude dependence parameters was incorporated into the final catalog in 1989.  To understand the complexity of the data analysis that led to this break from traditional astrometry, a overview is provided along with key insights into the shape of the hypothetical parallax curve and its implications for catalog development.  The impact of expanding data sets on the EUCOS model is discussed as well as the challenges in creating a new combined catalog.

This research expands on recent findings in model reduction, introducing two significant concepts. Firstly, it demonstrates how exponential growth in the growth of a function can be leveraged to enhance the DRx algorithm's speed, making it more efficient by a factor of n. Secondly, it shows how non-linear system equations can be simplified to a linear form, allowing the CRB algorithm's complexity to change from O(n^3) to a manageable level. These advancements are illustrated with a variety of examples, including a nonlinear beam, Duffing oscillator, nonlinear pendulum, and S-L-B problem.

We investigate a one-dimensional binary Bose-Einstein condensate consisting of two atom types with weakly repulsive and strongly repulsive atom-atom interactions in an optical lattice. By accurately accounting for non-degenerate ground and excited states, including both bosonic and fermionic states, we achieve a precise description. Our analysis focuses on stationary states formed by the balance of opposite forces, specifically in a binary mixture with contrasting interaction strengths. For weakly and strongly bound pairs, we derive accurate expressions for internal binding energies. Our study also reveals the stability of solitary waves, or solitons, in various excited states, even when subjected to strong external repulsion.

We introduce a novel approach for implementing fully-homomorphic parallel computation on encrypted data, with applications in secure machine learning inference. A key element of this approach is a new encoding technique for integer numbers, enabling efficient comparison and bitwise operations. This method supports comparing numbers up to 2^128 while requiring storage for only 64 times the original data, as well as adding homomorphic batch processing. By integrating this technique with integer-computations, we increase security ML inference capacity by 1.5x, a kx speedup in comparison to standard FHE-based secure computations, and enable computation for larger datasets in a single encrypted integer comparison.

Using data from HI4PI, researchers mapped the neutral hydrogen within the Local Group, discovering numerous HI points of interest both within and outside galaxies. These discoveries include possible HI branches connecting the M31 and M31 group, as well as newly identified HI clouds near and within the Milky Way and M31. Some of these clusters, including HI clouds surrounding the M80 and NGC 185 globular clusters in M31, may provide valuable information about the groups' accretion history and dynamical evolution. Additionally, some cloud candidates may represent distant HI structures that appear to be located within galaxy clusters when analyzed using redshift alone.

Full electronic structure for complex chemical species like CrO+ remains challenging to calculate. Although previous studies on similar, simpler species have been successful, doing so for crO+ is largely unexplored. The current work aims to break this barrier by using a combined approach to obtain a complete electronic structure for crO+ without these limitations. The method involves using the potential curve equations to map the potential energy surface, and then using the ABC code to get the potential curve in its natural format. The results from this study provide a detailed potential curve for crO+ that can be used in further investigations, and the data is made available online for ease of access.

A mathematical computation method has been developed that can break down specific types of complex numbers or algebraic numbers into the sum of squared components within their respective algebraic structures. This algorithm, which follows the general steps of its more specialized versions, uses a set of functions that are tailored to each specific case. The first of these functions, which applies to both types of numbers, is based on a set of explicit criteria that guide the process of finding the components. The method for complex numbers involves a direct formula, while the approach for algebraic numbers uses an alternative method with a clear set of limitations.

The measured correlation lag, along with its variance, can be a valuable tool for synchronizing streams of data from various telescopes. This synchronization allows for the calculation of time delays between events, which in turn, can provide insights into the timing differences of signals detected by each telescope.

As relational machine learning models start to see widespread use in pharmaceutical research, there's an urgent need to establish effective methods for assessing their performance. This review aims to examine the literature on the evaluation of message passing neural frameworks used in graph convolutional drug polypharmacy models. Currently, no comprehensive comparison or benchmark is available for these models. After a thorough analysis of 37 studies, several key evaluation strategies and metrics were identified and discussed. The main findings indicate that most studies evaluate model performance using average predictions rather than individual samples, result mostly on public datasets with limited diversity, and often assess relevant side effects but with insufficient depth. The study's outcome is a set of recommendations for future research to improve the evaluation of these models' performance.

A random walk-based method is proposed for federated learning to reduce the mixing time of stochastic learning while avoiding data transmission. By exploiting local computing power, each node performs stochastic gradient learning during a walk, with model updates only being shared with neighbors at adjacent locations. This method was tested in a image classification task and demonstrates improved efficiency and effectiveness over conventional FL approaches.

Fluid dynamics in rotating conditions exhibit intricate turbulence behavior.  
Previous research suggested that inertial waves may stabilize turbulent flows but  
lacked quantitative evidence regarding inertial wave characteristics.  
This study employs direct numerical simulations to show that turbulent flows at high  
Reynolds numbers confirm a $-2$ spectral density for inertial waves, consistent with  
previous theoretical estimates.  
Notably, this research is the first to provide rigorous proof that the inertial  
wave spectrum matches that proposed by Babulal and Balasubramanian and congruent  
with the predictions of Korotkov et al.  
Consequently, this finding signifies that rotating turbulence conforms to a specific  
wave turbulence framework, characterized by the dispersal of inertial waves.

Investing in treatment to address individuals' issues is vital for multiple reasons.  By examining administrative data from the city of B, we reveal the impact of mental health treatment on repeat offending and treatment requirements among individuals identified as high-risk repeat offenders.  As mental health treatment is largely determined by factors unrelated to crime in this specific context, we discover that completion of treatment reduces repeat crime by 21-36 percent and increases other individuals' treatment requirements by 22 percent, with these effects being more pronounced in certain sub-groups.  Our research reveals that repeat crime reduction resulting from treatment is primarily driven by a 27 percent decline in violent crimes and a 45 percent decline in serious personal crimes such as rape and murder among treated individuals, and we conclude that the increased crime rates observed for property crimes are compensatory in nature.  Our research also indicates that the effects of treatment on repeat crime are directed entirely at treated individuals with no spillover effects on other individuals in the community.  By comparing treated individuals to those who undergo treatment but do not finish the treatment program, we discover that repeat crime reduction resulting from treatment are accompanied by an increase in treatment requirements among other individuals by 22 percent.  Our research suggests that the positive effects of treatment on reducing crime are hindered by the high cost of providing such treatment. A novel approach to preventing overfitting in deep learning models for medical image segmentation has been proposed. Our method utilizes interpolation-based mixing as a regularization technique in semi-supervised learning, combining a small amount of pixel-wise mixing of unlabeled data with a high-weight technique. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, various experiments were conducted on three public datasets using two types of segmentation networks. Our results show that our proposed method consistently outperforms other techniques, including contrastive learning-based methods. Additionally, our method achieves optimal performance as the mixing factor is set to 0.5.

The Future Circular Collider (FCC), a proposed upgrade to the Large Hadron Collider, will necessitate significant enhancements to the detector and its associated computing system. One such upgrade will involve replacing the readout electronics for jets with a custom field-programmable gate array-based system called the jET readout module (jETmod). With the ability to process up to 100 terabytes of data per second, the FCC will allow for highly sophisticated jet analysis and, ultimately, potential discoveries of supersymmetry. To achieve this level of performance, the jETmod system will involve a highly optimized, multi-layered approach to data processing and signal reconstruction. This approach includes a combination of firmware, custom application software, and a highly efficient reconstruction algorithm that can keep up with the massive data rates expected from the FCC. In this paper, we present a detailed simulation of how this system will work, demonstrating its ability to accurately reconstruct jets and reproduce standard physics results from the existing detector. With some minor increases in resource requirements, our simulation achieves a match in performance to the original data, proving that this approach can successfully handle the massive data rates expected from the FCC.

Recent advancements in 3D image rendering have been driven by differentiable neural rendering frameworks that translate 3D geometric models and image plans into optical properties, ultimately enabling the creation of realistic dynamic scene visuals. However, most existing frameworks are limited to rendering static geometric shapes and fail to account for complex deformations induced by physical forces or optical effects. While research exists on inferring optical properties from 2D image sequences, it requires numerous assumptions and often results in illogical outcomes. By leveraging the interconnected nature of geometry and optics, our proposed AR framework utilizes a unified, fully differentiable pipeline to simultaneously model optical and geometric transformations, eliminating unnecessary assumptions and yielding more accurate results. Notably, our approach removes the need for projection algorithms, enabling a more direct translation from volumetric models to 2D images and yielding novel lighting effects. Through the utilization of modern physical-based rendering algorithms, our framework produces more accurate and visually appealing results compared to the industry standard. Additionally, our approach enables the efficient inference of optical properties from as few as 10 images, in contrast to the 10+ million pixels required by previous research.

Advanced graph neural network methods have successfully quantified local atomic environments in materials by leveraging the symmetry of convolutional neural networks and the invariance of set neural networks. However, current approaches have not incorporated physical principles such as the conservation of momentum and angular momentum. In this study, we propose a new invariant descriptor that integrates these principles for describing local atomic configurations. We demonstrate through experiments that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art descriptors in their ability to reconstruct electronic structure and atomic position data.

The article examines conditions under which weak convergence occurs for a specific class of parameters, characterized by the parameter space $\Theta$. Specifically, conditions are set for estimating functions of parameters, denoted as $\tau(\theta)$, and conditions are also established for estimating nested models, referred to as $M_n$.

Despite significant advancements in deep learning-based knowledge tracing, consensus on the best applications of this approach has not been reached. Moreover, comprehensive evaluations of these models are hindered by the labor-intensive nature of generating comparable datasets. In this study, we automate the comparison of knowledge tracing models through a diverse set of experiments, utilizing a newly created, widely accessible dataset. Our results indicate that the leading models, including our novel proposal, the Tridual Tracer, generally outperform their competitors. Additionally, our experiments on model efficiency and comparative analysis of active and non-recurrent models provide valuable insights into the current state of knowledge tracing, ultimately guiding future research in this domain.

The veriT proof format has been used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the veriT optimization-based solver in solving SMT problems, providing transparency into the solver's decision-making process. Since the PxTP workshop in 2009, improvements to this format have made it possible to represent the problems submitted to the SMT-COMP competition and the Theorem Prover PxTP workshop. Although the format's design allows for representation of these complex problems, some key features have not yet been implemented, and verifying the correctness of the generated proofs remains challenging. As a result, the authors have produced a new specification of the proof format, along with a corresponding implementation in C++, available on GitHub. This new specification aims to enable the representation of a broader range of problems and enhance the accuracy of generated outputs.

In the context of federated learning, two primary concerns arise: scalability and personal data protection. The FedBuff framework is introduced as a blockchain-based approach that enhances both objectives. Similar to a cache, FedBuff stores the update blocks contributed by mobile users, with the FFLServer selectively utilizing certain buffered updates for model training, thereby scaling FFL and enhancing its security. A comprehensive set of policies has been established for managing FedBuff, addressing issues such as optimal server selection, performance analysis, and clear conditions for model convergence. Analytical performance evaluations and simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of FedBuff in tackling both scalability and security challenges.

Deep neural network-based speech recognition technology has achieved major breakthroughs, but the high financial cost of collecting annotated audio data for training has been a limiting factor. Researchers have explored using transfer learning to utilize open-source audio data for pre-training models on one language and then adapting them to train models on other languages. This study aims to evaluate transfer learning models for speech recognition, focusing on transferring from English to Polish. It investigates both increasing the model size and experimenting with different target languages, including languages with high and low similarity. The results show that increasing model size leads to notable gains in accuracy but also increases model complexity. Moreover, it was discovered that models work best when transferring from English to languages with high similarity, but performance drops significantly when transferring to languages with low similarity. The experiments also indicated that both increasing the model size and choosing the target language affect how much of the English knowledge can be successfully transferred.

To assess novel node embedding methods, we developed a standard evaluation framework, 
which we applied to 15 state-of-the-art algorithms by creating five benchmark tests. 
These tests evaluate the predictive accuracy of nodes' attributes, classifications, 
edgelines, seizures, and a combination of all those aspects. 
Our experimental results, presented in this article, provide a clear comparison 
of current state-of-the-art algorithms, though further evaluation metrics are needed 
to fully judge node embeddings, as mentioned in this article.

A study of the $B^+ \to K^+ K_S K_S$ decay, consisting of $B^+ \to K^+ f_0(500)$ and $B^+ \to K^+ f_0(980)$ $S$-wave contributions, is presented. We observed a broad structure near the $B^+$ mass in the $K_S K_S$ invariant mass spectrum within the $S$-wave component, with a significant significance of 4.6 standard deviations, having a expected p-value of 0.0000036, considering both statistical and systematic uncertainties. We interpreted this structure as potentially indicating the existence of a broad $B^+ \to K^+ f_0(1370)$ resonance. As a result, we set a 90% confidence level upper limit of 6.7 times 10^-7 for the $B^+ \to K^+ f_0(1370)$ branching fraction.

The non-baryonic nature of dark matter has yet to be definitively proven. 
Recently observed excesses in the cosmic and anti-cosmic neutron spectra might 
offer a route for detecting dark matter Primordial Black Holes (PBHs). Under 
the assumption that dark matter consists entirely of primordial black holes in the 
mass range of 1-100 solar masses, this study offers an alternative explanation 
for the observed excess events. It is forecasted that if this PBH dark matter 
scenario is correct, more significant signals will appear in the coming years 
with existing and future detectors. Nevertheless, it should be noted that the 
PBH dark matter hypothesis is only marginally consistent with current constraints 
and may be further limited by observations of gravitational waves, as well 
as electromagnetic and gravitational constraints. This study offers a comprehensive 
overview of the primordial black hole dark matter hypothesis and presents updated 
and more accurate predictions that can be compared with existing and future 
datasets to validate the feasibility of this scenario.

Series elastic actuators utilize a compliant component before a force sensor to make measuring robotic forces more accurate and reliable. Despite their advantages, accurately measuring force in these actuators is a complex task, as it must account for nonlinearity and sensor inaccuracies. Additionally, determining force involves integrating acceleration measurements, which are affected by sensor inaccuracies and result in accumulating errors. To tackle these challenges, this paper presents a nonlinear filter that provides a robust estimate of force in SEAs by combining the benefits of both actuators. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, simulations and physical experiments have been performed.

The interaction between expanding fluids and aggregating particles can lead to diverse patterns with potential applications in self-assembly and terraforming. As the fluid increases in size, particles are pushed apart; however, if the fluid closes up, they can continue to cluster. We studied the dynamics of a two-dimensional raft consisting of ethanol-filled water menisci and colloidal polystyrene spheres suspended within, discovering that the raft suddenly jumps to a larger size when the solvent is removed and the raft's area shrinks below a critical threshold. This unexpected increase in the raft's size is attributed to an increase in the menisci's curvature. To understand the relationship between the menisci expansion and particle aggregation competition, we developed a theoretical model. It reveals that the distance between adjacent rifts results from this competition and that the raft's age influences its ability to maintain its integrity. Notably, the raft can stay connected to a critical age, causing it to abruptly jump to a larger size when the raft passes beyond this age, further confirming our findings experimentally.

The study of multi-component complex scalar fields takes a new direction in this work. In the case of two-component fields on a 2D lattice, it is shown that distinct phases result in a permanent mass gap or gap reduction in the continuum limit. This is influenced by a unitary symmetry property. It is also demonstrated that a 2D lattice model's unitary symmetry leads to three distinct phases, which can be differentiated by their effective cosmological constants. This is in contrast to the U(1) symmetric case, which results in a first-order phase transition between the symmetric and broken phases. Furthermore, it is shown that a U(1) N-rotational symmetric model's critical point lies at the boundary between the broken and symmetric phases. This is in contrast to an asymmetric model, which has been previously studied and shown to have a second-order phase transition at a specific critical value of N. This is in contrast to a model with unitary or U(1) N-rotational symmetry, which has been shown to have a second-order phase transition at a specific critical value of N. This is in contrast to a model with unitary or U(1) N-rotational symmetry, which has been shown to have a second-order phase transition at a specific critical value of N.

The GP-based policy evaluation algorithm known as SPGP-SARSA has been utilized for underwater navigation tasks in previous studies. By integrating a sparse approximation of the value function, this approach achieves a significant reduction in memory requirements, enabling real-time computation on modest hardware. However, existing applications of SPGP-SARSA are limited to state spaces composed of grid states and continuous domains governed by simple dynamic rules. In this study, we expand the applicability of SPGP-SARSA to more complex state spaces and broadly applicable system dynamics. Our experiments indicate that SPGP-SARSA maintains its convergence and performance benefits under these broader conditions.

We have derived new upper bounds for the minimal comparison count of sorting networks as a function of circuit depth, specifically for depths 1 to 4. At depth 3, our findings reconcile with the established limits set by Krapivnyi and Benes in 2016. However, at depths 2 and 4, our results show significant deviation, offering up to $O(n)$ and $O(n^{1/4})$ improvements respectively. Moreover, our research establishes a striking contrast, as the minimal arity of sorting networks at depths 3 and 4 stands in opposition to that at depths 1 and 2.

Building upon a previous study by the author and others, I constructed a new class of analytic, relativistic stellar models consisting of two fluids. These models were created by dividing a Bardeen equation of state fluid into two components with distinct pressures and densities. The process of constructing the models involved using dimensionless variables and a specific function, $y^2 = f(x)$, to define the density of the Bardeen fluid. The surface of the stellar body was determined using the root of a specific equation, and the model's composition was illustrated through dimensionless composition fractions. I also explored a specific case by assuming a specific form for $x$ and calculated the surface radius and central densities for both fluid components. The results showed that the model can accurately represent neutron stars when assuming a specific shape for $x$. Additionally, using the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, I calculated gravitational redshifts at the surface of the star and found that they fell within the observed range for known neutron stars.

We investigated how bars form in galactic disks with varying density distributions, specifically in Kuhn-Poisson and exponential forms, using N-body simulations and a stability analysis. Our findings show that the bar's shape is influenced by the density distribution's scale length, particularly in outer regions where bars may not form in exponential disks but can in Poisson disks. A quadruple resonance analysis also indicates that the bar's formation is affected by the density distribution's scale length, and inner bars can merge with outer ones in Poisson disks to form a unified bar near the Lindstedt resonance.

The ultimate fate of merger remnants from gas-rich major galactic collisions is heavily influenced by magnetic fields. To explore this, we ran hydrodynamic simulations without gravity, in two scenarios - one with and one without magnetic fields - following the collisions, to compare their outcomes. We compared the results at various stages, looking for signs of magnetic field suppression, and observed the formation of merger remnant structures. In the absence of magnetic fields, these structures arise solely from gas dynamics. However, when magnetic fields are present, they induce additional structure within the remnant, especially along its boundaries. The results show that while magnetic fields are partially suppressed as the remnant forms and contracts, they ultimately enhance the efficiency of angular momentum transport and promote more effective mixing and cooling, leading to increased star and magnetic field formation rates within the remnant. This process is especially evident in remnants with higher initial magnetic fields. Gas collisions also play a crucial role in this process, leading to the creation of shock layers, tidal streams, and spherical shells, which are sites of star and magnetic field formation. Our findings highlight that magnetic fields are an integral component of merger remnant morphology and cannot be regarded as a afterthought.

This research develops a novel 3D contrastive learning framework, referred to as CB3D, which employs contrastive learnable layers and transforms raw 3D CT lung images into low-dimensional feature representations. Furthermore, an improved CB3D model, called mCB3D, is presented which incorporates a dynamic sampling technique to address the challenge of unbalanced data distribution. Our experiments indicate that both models achieve superior performance compared to existing methods in lung cancer severity classification. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of the proposed method through successful clinical applications and data ablation experiments.
